title: Mass extinctions: how most kinds of life ended five times, how life came back, and what is happening now

summary.text: Five times, most of the kinds of living beings on Earth died out in a short time. Yet after each of those times, life filled the world again. How did so few survivors do that, and how long did it take? In this lesson you wipe out a paper world with coins and refill it with a die. You also roll for fossils in a paper cliff, to see why a sudden ending can look slow in the rocks. Then you compare the extinctions of today with the five great ones.
summary.art: A paper grid of 36 squares on a table, most squares rubbed out, with a coin, a die and a pencil beside it, and a crow watching from the window grill.

intro.hook: Big dinosaurs filled the land for more than 130 million years. Mammals lived beside them all that time, and almost all stayed smaller than a cat. Then the big dinosaurs ended, and within about ten million years there were mammals as big as cows. Why did the mammals wait so long, and what let them change so fast?
intro.text: You already know that fossils are traces of old life, and that the big dinosaurs died out. In this lesson you go further. You find out that dying out is normal, and that most kinds that ever lived are gone. You learn about the five times when most kinds ended together. These are called mass extinctions. You test with coins and a die how a nearly empty world fills up again, and who fills it. You find out why the last fossil of an animal is almost never the last animal. Then you look at today. Kinds are ending faster now than is normal, and scientists argue about how to name what is happening.
intro.art: A child drawing a long paper time line on the floor, with five red marks along it and a small sketch of a trilobite, an ammonite and a dinosaur above three of the marks.

outcomes: By the end I can explain the difference between background extinction and a mass extinction.
By the end I can put the five mass extinctions in order and give a likely cause for at least three.
By the end I can use my Empty Board Test to explain how life refills the world, and why that takes millions of years.
By the end I can explain who lived through the asteroid strike of 66 million years ago, and why.
By the end I can explain why the last fossil found is not the last animal, using my Last Fossil Test.
By the end I can give the evidence for the asteroid and for the Deccan volcanoes, and say what is still argued.
By the end I can compare today's extinction rate with the normal rate, and say honestly what is known.

terms.meaning: A species is one kind of living being. Members of a species can have young together, and their young can have young too.
terms.example: The house crow and the jungle crow look alike, but they are two species. The Asian elephant is one species.
terms.art: A house crow with a grey neck beside an all-black jungle crow on a wall.

terms.meaning: Extinction is the end of a species. It happens when the last member dies and none are left anywhere.
terms.example: The dodo of Mauritius is extinct. The last sure sighting of a living dodo was in 1662.
terms.art: A dodo standing on a forest floor, drawn in faded colours.

terms.meaning: Background extinction is the slow, steady ending of species that goes on all the time. A few species end in every stretch of a million years.
terms.example: A snail species that lives in one lake dies out when the lake dries over thousands of years. Nothing else in the world changes.
terms.art: A long row of many small animal shapes, with one shape here and there faded out.

terms.meaning: A mass extinction is a time when most species on Earth die out in a short stretch of time. Many scientists use the measure of three out of every four species gone within about two million years.
terms.example: About 66 million years ago, about three out of four species died out. The big dinosaurs and the ammonites were among them.
terms.art: The same long row of animal shapes, with three out of every four faded out at one point.

terms.meaning: The fossil record is all the fossils that have been found, together with the rock layers they lie in. It is our only direct record of life long ago.
terms.example: The rocks around Ariyalur in Tamil Nadu hold shells of sea animals. They are part of the record of a sea that was there in the time of the dinosaurs.
terms.art: A cliff of striped rock layers with a few shells and bones showing in different layers.

terms.meaning: A boundary layer is a thin layer of rock that marks the change from one age to the next. The fossils below it differ from the fossils above it.
terms.example: A thin layer of clay, about as thick as a finger, marks the end of the age of dinosaurs in rocks around the world.
terms.art: A close view of a cliff with a thin dark line of clay between pale rock below and pale rock above.

terms.meaning: Iridium is a rare metal. Earth's surface rocks hold very little of it, and asteroids hold much more.
terms.example: The clay layer from 66 million years ago holds far more iridium than the rocks above and below. That was the first clue to an asteroid strike.
terms.art: A scientist's gloved hand holding a small piece of grey clay over a tray.

terms.meaning: A flood basalt is a huge sheet of lava that poured out of long cracks in the ground, again and again, over thousands of years. Basalt is the dark rock that the lava became.
terms.example: The Deccan Traps of Maharashtra are a flood basalt. The flat-topped, stepped hills around Mahabaleshwar are layers of that lava.
terms.art: Flat-topped stepped hills of dark rock in the Western Ghats, with green on each step.

terms.meaning: Ocean acidification means the sea becoming more acid. It happens when a lot of the gas carbon dioxide dissolves in sea water. Animals then find it harder to build shells.
terms.example: Soda water is water with carbon dioxide dissolved in it. It tastes a little sour because the gas makes a weak acid.
terms.art: A glass of soda water with bubbles beside a sea snail shell.

terms.meaning: Detritus is dead plant and animal matter, such as fallen leaves, rotting wood and dead bodies.
terms.example: Earthworms, millipedes and many insects eat detritus. They can keep feeding even when no plant is growing.
terms.art: A millipede and an earthworm among brown fallen leaves.

terms.meaning: A niche is one way of making a living in one kind of place. It covers what a species eats, where they live and when they are active.
terms.example: Eating leaves from the tops of tall trees is a niche. Giraffes fill that niche in Africa today. Long-necked dinosaurs filled a niche like that once.
terms.art: A giraffe eating from a treetop, with a faint outline of a long-necked dinosaur doing the same behind.

terms.meaning: Recovery is the time after a mass extinction when the number of species grows again. New species arise from the survivors.
terms.example: After the big dinosaurs ended, the number of mammal species grew for millions of years.
terms.art: A bare grey landscape on the left turning into a green one full of animals on the right.

terms.meaning: An adaptive radiation is the splitting of one group into many new species in a fairly short time, each fitted to a different niche. It often happens when many niches are empty.
terms.example: After 66 million years ago, small mammals gave rise to bats, whales, horses, elephants and many more.
terms.art: A small shrew-like animal at the bottom, with lines branching up to a bat, a whale, a horse and an elephant.

terms.meaning: A Lazarus species is a species that people thought was extinct and then found alive. The name comes from an old story about a man who came back from death.
terms.example: Jerdon's courser is a bird of Andhra Pradesh. No scientist saw one from 1900 to 1986. Then one was found alive near Kadapa.
terms.art: A small brown bird with two dark bands on the chest, standing in dry scrub at night in the light of a torch.

terms.meaning: The extinction rate is how many species end in a given time, out of a given number of species.
terms.example: One estimate of the normal rate is 2 extinctions among 10,000 species in 100 years.
terms.art: A notebook page with a tally of species lost beside a calendar of one hundred years.

terms.term: Extinct in the wild, and extinct in one country
terms.meaning: A species is extinct in the wild when the only ones left live in zoos or farms. A species can also be gone from one country and still live in another.
terms.example: Cheetahs were declared extinct in India in 1952. Cheetahs still lived in Africa and in Iran.
terms.art: A map of India with a faded cheetah on it, and a bright cheetah on a map of Africa beside it.

explanations.concept: Background extinction: species are always ending
explanations.definition: Background extinction is the slow ending of species, a few at a time, that goes on in every age.
explanations.description: No species lasts for ever. In the fossil record, a species usually lasts between one million and ten million years. Mammal species often last only one to three million years. Then the species ends, or changes so much that scientists give the descendants a new name. Why does a species end? A lake dries. A new predator arrives. A rival eats the same food and does it better. The climate shifts and the forest the species needs turns to grassland. While some species end, others split into new ones, so the number of species stays roughly level or slowly rises. Scientists estimate that more than 99 out of every 100 species that ever lived are now extinct. That is an estimate, because most species left no fossils at all. So extinction is the usual end of a species. It does not mean the species did something wrong.
examples: In the Hundred Squares activity, you colour only 1 square out of 100 for the species alive today.
Trilobites were sea animals with jointed armour. Thousands of trilobite species came and went over about 270 million years. Each species lasted a few million years.
Our own species, Homo sapiens, is about 300,000 years old. That is young for a species.
explanations.art: A branching bush drawn sideways, with most twigs ending in a small cross and a few reaching the right edge.

explanations.concept: Mass extinctions: the five great ones
explanations.definition: A mass extinction is a time when most species on Earth die out within a short stretch of geological time, all over the world and in many groups at once.
explanations.description: In 1982 two scientists in Chicago, David Raup and Jack Sepkoski, counted the fossil families of sea animals through time. Sepkoski had spent years gathering the list from books and papers. Their graph showed the number of kinds slowly rising, with five sharp drops. People now call them the Big Five. Each one killed about three quarters of all species or more. The percentages are estimates, and different studies give different numbers. Each of the five had a different cause, but the causes share something. In each one the air, the sea or the climate changed faster than living beings could keep up with. Later counts show some smaller drops too. So the Big Five are the largest of many extinction events. They are not a separate kind of event.
examples: End of the Ordovician, about 444 million years ago. Great ice sheets grew and the sea level fell, then rose again. Almost all life was in the sea then. About 85 out of 100 species ended.

Late Devonian, about 370 million years ago. This one came in several steps over a long time. Sea life was hit hardest. The causes are still argued. One idea is that the first forests changed the air and cooled the Earth.
End of the Permian, about 252 million years ago. Huge volcanoes in Siberia heated the Earth and made the sea acid. This was the worst of all.
End of the Triassic, about 201 million years ago. The land began to split where the Atlantic Ocean is now, and lava poured out. Afterwards, dinosaurs became the main large land animals.
End of the Cretaceous, about 66 million years ago. An asteroid struck, and the Deccan volcanoes were erupting. About 3 out of 4 species ended.
explanations.art: A line graph of the number of kinds of sea animals over 540 million years, rising overall with five sharp dips marked by small red arrows.

explanations.concept: The worst one: the end of the Permian
explanations.definition: The end-Permian extinction, about 252 million years ago, is the largest extinction known. About 8 out of 10 species in the sea ended, and about 7 out of 10 species of land animals with backbones.
explanations.description: In what is now Siberia, lava poured out of the ground over a huge area. The eruptions sent enormous amounts of carbon dioxide into the air. Carbon dioxide is a gas that traps heat, so the Earth warmed by several degrees. Much of the gas dissolved in the sea and made the water more acid. Animals who build shells and skeletons from the minerals in sea water could no longer build them well. Warm water also holds less oxygen, so large parts of the sea had too little oxygen to breathe. On land, many places dried out. The main die-off took about 60,000 years. That sounds long. But against the age of the Earth it is very short, like one second in a whole day. Older books say 96 out of 100 sea species died. Newer counts give about 81, because an earlier, separate extinction had been mixed in. The trilobites ended for ever. So did many groups of corals and sea lilies. Even insects, who came through the other mass extinctions well, lost many groups.
examples: After this extinction, one plant-eater about the size of a pig was the most common land animal with a backbone for a time. This animal is called Lystrosaurus. In some rock beds of South Africa, about 95 out of 100 fossils of land animals with backbones are Lystrosaurus.
Lystrosaurus fossils are also found in India, in the Panchet rocks of the Damodar valley in West Bengal and Jharkhand. India, Africa and Antarctica were joined in one land then.
Sea life took about 10 million years to become rich again. Land animals with backbones took even longer.
explanations.art: A dry, cracked plain under a hazy orange sky, with a stout tusked animal the size of a pig digging at the foot of a dead tree.

explanations.concept: The end of the Cretaceous: the asteroid and the Deccan volcanoes
explanations.definition: About 66 million years ago, about three quarters of all species died out. An asteroid about 10 kilometres wide struck where Mexico is now, at a time when the Deccan volcanoes of India were erupting.
explanations.description: The asteroid strike is not in doubt. It left a buried crater about 180 to 200 kilometres wide, called Chicxulub. It left a thin layer of clay rich in iridium all over the world. It also left grains of quartz with tiny cracks that only a huge shock can make. Dust and soot blocked the sunlight. Computer models suggest the dark lasted from some months to about two years. Without light, plants and the tiny floating algae of the sea could not make food, so food chains broke from the bottom. The Deccan eruptions are not in doubt either. Their lava still covers about 500,000 square kilometres of western and central India. Volcanic gases can warm the Earth and make rain and sea water acid. The argument is about which of the two did most of the killing. Dating the lava is hard. Two teams dated it in 2019 with two methods, and their answers did not agree on when the biggest eruptions came.
examples: At Anjar in Kutch, Gujarat, layers rich in iridium lie in lake mud between Deccan lava flows. So lava was already flowing in India before the asteroid's dust settled there.
In Meghalaya, the rocks beside the Um Sohryngkew River hold a layer with much more iridium than the layers around it.
Rajasaurus was a meat-eating dinosaur about as long as a small bus. Their bones were found at Rahioli in Gujarat, in rocks from the last few million years before the end.

perspectives.explanation: The asteroid was the main cause. In 2010 a group of 41 scientists reviewed twenty years of evidence and came to this view. In 2020 a study of old sea temperatures found that the big changes fit the time of the strike, not the eruptions.

perspectives.who: Gerta Keller of Princeton University and her co-workers
perspectives.explanation: The Deccan eruptions were the main cause. Keller has studied tiny sea fossils for decades. She argues that many species were already in trouble before the strike.
The eruptions had already put life under strain, and the asteroid then did most of the killing. Many scientists think both mattered and still argue about the shares.

explanations.art: A split picture: on the left a glowing streak falling towards a blue sea, on the right long cracks in dark ground pouring out red lava under a smoky sky.

explanations.concept: Who lived through the asteroid strike, and why
explanations.definition: A mass extinction does not kill at random. At the end of the Cretaceous, survival depended mostly on body size, on food and on shelter.
explanations.description: On land, almost no animal with a backbone heavier than about 25 kilograms survived. A large animal needs a lot of food every day, and there was almost none. Animals who fed on living plants died, and so did the meat-eaters who fed on them. Many survivors belonged to food chains that begin with detritus. Insects, worms and snails ate dead leaves and rotting wood. Small mammals, small birds, lizards and frogs ate the insects, worms and snails. Animals who could shelter in burrows or under water came through the first heat and the cold that followed. Seeds and spores could wait in the soil. Rivers and lakes did better than the open sea, because dead matter washing in from the land kept feeding them. So the features that had made a species successful stopped helping. Great size had been an advantage for millions of years, and now it was a danger. Small size, a wide diet and a hiding place had been ordinary features, and now they mattered most. Luck mattered too. Many small mammal species and most kinds of birds also died.
examples: Crocodiles and turtles are an exception to the size rule. They live in water and can go for months without food.
Among birds, the survivors seem to have been ground-living birds. One explanation is that the forests burned or died, so tree-living birds lost their homes.
In the sea, the ammonites died out. They were shelled relatives of squids, and their young floated among the tiny algae. The nautilus, a relative who lives in deep water, survived and is still alive.
The first plants to cover the bare ground were ferns. Fern spores are so common in the rock just above the clay layer that scientists call it the fern spike.
explanations.art: A dark, smoky forest floor with fallen trunks, where a small furry mammal looks out of a burrow, a millipede crosses a dead leaf and fern shoots uncurl.

explanations.concept: Recovery: how a nearly empty world fills up again
explanations.definition: Recovery is the growth in the number of species after a mass extinction. The survivors spread, and over a very long time their descendants split into many new species that fill the empty niches.
explanations.description: A mass extinction leaves many niches empty. Nobody eats the tall leaves, and nobody hunts in the shallow sea. A world full of species leaves little room for a new one, because a new kind must do a job better than someone who already does it. An emptied world is different. The survivors meet few rivals, so many of their varieties can live and have young. Over many thousands of generations, natural selection fits different groups of descendants to different niches, and one species becomes many. This is an adaptive radiation. It is fast compared with normal times, and still very slow for us. A study by James Kirchner and Anne Weil in 2000 looked at the whole fossil record of sea life. The number of species took about 10 million years to recover after an extinction, whether the extinction was large or small. The lost species never come back. New and different species take their places.
examples: In your Empty Board Test, no group can add a species while the board is full. After the extinction, the survivors fill the board in a few rounds, and the group marked D never returns.

At Corral Bluffs in Colorado, fossils show the first million years after the asteroid. The mammal survivors were about the size of a rat. About 100,000 years later there were mammals of about 6 kilograms. After about 700,000 years, some weighed nearly 50 kilograms.
Mammals were not the only winners. Today there are more than 6,000 species of mammals and about 11,000 species of birds. Birds are dinosaurs, so the age of dinosaurs has not fully ended.
Some groups survive a mass extinction and then fade away in the next few million years. Scientists call such a group a 'dead clade walking'. A clade is one branch of the family tree of life.
explanations.art: Three panels left to right: a grey plain with ferns and one rat-sized mammal, then young forest with a raccoon-sized mammal, then tall forest with a calf-sized mammal.

explanations.concept: The last fossil is not the last animal
explanations.definition: The last fossil found of a species almost always comes from some time before the species really ended. The rarer the fossils, the bigger the gap is likely to be.
explanations.description: Very few animals become fossils, and people find only a few of those. So the youngest fossil of a species is the last one that was buried, kept and found. The real last animal lived later, and sometimes much later. Two scientists, Philip Signor and Jere Lipps, pointed out what follows from this in 1982. Suppose many species die on the same day. The common ones leave fossils right up to that day. The rare ones leave their last fossil well below it. A person reading the cliff from the bottom up sees the species vanish one after another. A sudden ending looks like a slow one. This is called the Signor-Lipps effect. Your Last Fossil Test shows it with a die. The same effect works at the start of a species too. The first fossil found is later than the first animal.
examples: For years, the highest dinosaur bones found in the rocks of western North America lay about three metres below the iridium layer. Some scientists said the dinosaurs had gone before the asteroid. Wider searches later found bones closer to the layer.

In the 1980s Peter Ward studied ammonites in sea cliffs in Spain. At first they seemed to stop well below the boundary. After more years of searching in nearby cliffs, he found ammonites right up to it.
The fix is to search more rock, in more places, and to use maths to estimate the likely gap.
explanations.art: A cliff of twenty layers with a red line at the top, and five columns of fossil symbols that stop at different heights below the line.

explanations.definition: A Lazarus species is one that was thought extinct and was then found alive. Not being seen is weak evidence that a species is gone.
explanations.description: Scientists call a species extinct only when careful searches, in the right places and seasons, have failed for many years. The rule of the Red List, the world list of species at risk, is that there must be no reasonable doubt that the last one has died. This is hard to be sure of. A small animal who is active at night in thick scrub can be missed for a hundred years. So some species come back from the list of the lost. Finding one is a joy, and a warning as well. A species missed for a century is almost always very rare, and can still end soon.
examples: The coelacanth is a large fish with fleshy fins. The youngest fossils known were about 66 million years old, so scientists thought coelacanths had died out with the big dinosaurs. In 1938 Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer found a fresh one on a fishing boat in South Africa.

Jerdon's courser is a night bird of the scrub forest near Kadapa in Andhra Pradesh. The last record was in 1900. In January 1986 a bird trapper named Aitanna caught one, and Bharat Bhushan of the Bombay Natural History Society confirmed the find. The state then made the place a sanctuary. In August 2025 birdwatchers recorded the bird's call again, after more than fifteen years without a record.

The dodo is not a Lazarus species. People have searched the small island of Mauritius for more than 300 years. In about 1625, the Mughal court painter Ustad Mansur painted a living dodo. That painting is among the best pictures we have of the bird. DNA from a museum dodo shows that the Nicobar pigeon of India's Nicobar Islands is the closest living relative.
explanations.art: A woman in 1930s clothes on a fishing dock lifting a pile of small sharks to show a large blue fish with fleshy fins underneath.

explanations.definition: The extinction rate today is the number of species ending in our time, compared with the number that would end in normal times.
explanations.description: To know whether today is unusual, scientists compare two numbers. The first is the background rate from the fossil record. A careful study in 2015, led by Gerardo Ceballos in Mexico, used a high value for it on purpose, so as not to exaggerate. The value was 2 extinctions for every 10,000 species in 100 years. At that rate, about 9 species of animals with backbones should have ended since 1900. The second number is the count of real losses. On a cautious count, 477 such species are gone or very probably gone since 1900. That is about 50 times the normal number. Other studies give from tens of times to 1,000 times, because each method counts differently. The causes are known. People clear the places where species live, hunt and fish too much, carry species to new places, pollute, and heat the climate. Each cause is something people do, so people can also do less of it.
examples: In October 2025 the Red List had looked at 172,620 species. Of these, 48,646 were at risk of extinction. That is more than one in four of the species checked.
The passenger pigeon of North America once numbered in billions. Hunting and forest clearing ended them. The last one, a female named Martha, died in a zoo on 1 September 1914.
Most of the millions of species on Earth have never been checked. Most insects have not even been named.
explanations.art: Two bars side by side on a notebook page: a very short bar labelled 'normal' and a bar about fifty times taller labelled 'since 1900'.

explanations.concept: Are we in a sixth mass extinction?
explanations.definition: Scientists agree that species are ending much faster than normal because of what people do. They disagree about whether to call this a mass extinction yet.
explanations.description: A mass extinction, by the usual measure, means about three out of four species gone. Since the year 1500, fewer than 1,000 extinctions have been recorded, among well over a million named species. Many more have surely been missed. Even so, the losses so far are far below three out of four. The worry is the rate. If the rate stays as high as now, and the species at risk today are lost, the count could reach the level of the Big Five in some hundreds or thousands of years. In the life of the Earth that would be very sudden. So the two sides agree on most of the facts. They differ on which word fits them.
examples: In 2011 a team led by Anthony Barnosky wrote that the losses so far are serious, but do not yet make a mass extinction. They added that losing the species now at risk would bring one within a few centuries.
India shows both sides. The cheetah was lost from India by 1952. The tiger, the Asiatic lion and the one-horned rhinoceros were close to ending and have grown in number under protection.

perspectives.who: Gerardo Ceballos, Paul Ehrlich and co-workers (2015)
perspectives.explanation: A sixth mass extinction is already under way. The rate is far above normal, and waiting for three quarters of species to die before using the name would be waiting too long.

perspectives.who: Anthony Barnosky and co-workers (2011), and Stuart Pimm
perspectives.explanation: It has not happened yet. The rate is alarming, but most species are still here, so a mass extinction can still be prevented.
The fossil record mostly shows sea animals with shells, counted over millions of years. Today's counts are mostly of birds and mammals over a few hundred years. The two are hard to compare fairly.

explanations.art: A staircase going down with five deep steps labelled with ancient dates, and a sixth step only just begun, with people standing at its edge holding it up.

explanations.concept: If life's history ran again, would the same beings appear?
explanations.definition: Scientists ask whether the living world we have was bound to happen, or depends on accidents such as an asteroid strike.
explanations.description: If the asteroid had missed, big dinosaurs might still rule the land, and large mammals might never have appeared. That would mean no elephants, no whales and no humans. The way things turn out when they depend on accidents is called contingency. Other scientists point to convergence. Convergence means that unrelated animals often arrive at the same answer to the same problem. Nobody can run the history of life twice, so this stays an argument about evidence. Your Empty Board Test gives a small taste of it. Run it twice with the same rules, and a different group may end up with the most squares.
examples: Wings arose separately in insects, in the flying reptiles called pterosaurs, in birds and in bats.
Dolphins are mammals and ichthyosaurs were reptiles. Both ended up with the body shape of a fast fish.

perspectives.who: Stephen Jay Gould, in Wonderful Life (1989)
perspectives.explanation: Chance rules. Replay the tape of life from the start, and the result would be utterly different each time. Humans would almost surely not appear.

perspectives.who: Simon Conway Morris, in Life's Solution (2003)
perspectives.explanation: There are only so many good ways to make a living. Eyes, wings and large brains have arisen many times, so something like them would arise again.

explanations.art: Two branching trees growing from the same seed, the same height but with their branches going different ways.

explanations.concept: Following the idea further: atoms, the sky and what nobody knows
explanations.definition: The causes of mass extinctions reach from single atoms to the space around the Earth.
explanations.description: Start with atoms. A molecule of carbon dioxide is one carbon atom joined to two oxygen atoms. When it dissolves in water, it joins with a water molecule and makes a weak acid called carbonic acid. That one small reaction, repeated without number, made the end-Permian sea acid. It is happening again. Since about 1850 people have burned coal and oil, and the surface of the sea has become a little more acid. Next, energy. The asteroid was moving at many kilometres each second. When it stopped, its energy of movement turned into heat, shock and flying rock. Then the sky. The iridium in the clay layer came from space. Earth moves among countless rocks, and large strikes are very rare but not over. Space agencies now track the large rocks that pass near the Earth. Last, the open questions. Nobody knows why the Late Devonian extinction came in steps. Nobody knows how many species are alive today. Estimates run from a few million to many millions.
examples: In 2022 the DART spacecraft struck a small asteroid on purpose and changed its path a little. It was the first test of pushing an asteroid aside.
Soda water turns blue litmus paper red, because dissolved carbon dioxide makes carbonic acid.
explanations.art: A zoom from a carbon dioxide molecule beside a water molecule, out to a sea snail shell, out to the Earth with a small rock passing by.

agreed.text: Most species that have ever lived are extinct.
agreed.evidence: Rock layers of every age hold fossils of species that are not alive today. A species usually lasts a few million years in the record, and life is more than 3,500 million years old.

agreed.text: At least five times, most species died out within a short stretch of geological time.
agreed.evidence: Counts of fossil groups through the rock layers show five sharp drops. Raup and Sepkoski published the first such count in 1982, and later counts with far more fossils show the same five.

agreed.text: A large asteroid struck the Earth about 66 million years ago.
agreed.evidence: There is a buried crater in Mexico of that age. A layer rich in iridium, with shocked quartz, lies in rocks of that age around the world, including in India.

agreed.text: The end-Permian extinction happened at the time of huge eruptions in Siberia.
agreed.evidence: The lava and the extinction layer have been dated with uranium in tiny crystals. The dates match to within some tens of thousands of years.

agreed.text: After a mass extinction, new species arise from the survivors, and the lost species do not return.
agreed.evidence: The fossils above each extinction layer belong to different species from those below. No trilobite appears above the end-Permian layer anywhere.

agreed.text: Species are ending faster today than the normal rate, mainly because of what people do.
agreed.evidence: The recorded losses of birds, mammals, amphibians and other animals with backbones since 1900 are many times the number expected from the fossil record.

challenging.claim: The Deccan volcanoes of India, not the asteroid, were the main killer 66 million years ago.
challenging.who: Gerta Keller of Princeton University, with co-workers including Indian geologists
challenging.for: The eruptions were enormous and went on for hundreds of thousands of years. Some of the tiny sea fossils Keller studies seem to decline before the strike. In India, iridium lies between lava flows, so lava was flowing before the dust settled.
challenging.against: The best dates put the extinction at the time of the strike. A 2020 study of sea temperatures found the big changes at the strike, not at the eruptions. A decline before the strike may be partly the Signor-Lipps effect.
challenging.context: This card is about what killed the big dinosaurs and three quarters of all species 66 million years ago. Most scientists blame an asteroid, and some blame volcanoes in India.

challenging.claim: The dinosaurs were already dying out slowly before the asteroid came.
challenging.who: Many palaeontologists before the 1990s, and a few today
challenging.for: In some places fewer kinds of dinosaur bones are found in the last few million years before the end.
challenging.against: Rare fossils always seem to stop early. Careful searches in North America found dinosaur bones close to the boundary. Where the record is good, many kinds of dinosaurs lived right up to the end.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the big dinosaurs ended suddenly or slowly. The answer depends on how well we can read the last fossils.

challenging.claim: Mass extinctions come round every 26 million years or so, driven by something in space.
challenging.who: David Raup and Jack Sepkoski, in 1984
challenging.for: Their count of sea fossils seemed to show extinction peaks at regular gaps. Some astronomers suggested a faint companion star of the Sun that sends comets our way.
challenging.against: No such star has been found, though telescopes have searched the whole sky. Better dating of the rocks made the regular pattern much weaker.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea that mass extinctions arrive on a timetable. It was tested and most scientists gave it up.

challenging.claim: A sixth mass extinction has already begun.
challenging.who: Gerardo Ceballos, Paul Ehrlich and others, in 2015
challenging.for: Animals with backbones have been ending about 50 times faster than normal since 1900, on a cautious count. More than one in four of the species checked are at risk.
challenging.against: Fewer than 1 in 100 named species are recorded as lost so far. A mass extinction means about 3 in 4. So others say it is a danger ahead and has not happened yet.
challenging.context: This card is about the extinctions of our own time. Scientists agree the rate is far too high, and argue about what to call it.

challenging.claim: Extinction is natural, so losing species today does not matter.
challenging.who: A view often heard in arguments about protecting nature
challenging.for: It is true that extinction is the normal end of every species, and that life recovered after each mass extinction.
challenging.against: Recovery took about 10 million years each time. Our whole species is only about 300,000 years old. A lost species never returns. Also, today's losses have a cause that can choose to stop.
challenging.context: This card is about a common argument: species have always died out, so why worry now? The unit's own numbers answer it.

big_questions.q: In the Empty Board Test, the group that held most of the board was wiped out. Does being successful protect a species?
big_questions.hint: Think about what had made big dinosaurs successful, and what that same feature did in the dark months.

big_questions.q: If every kind dies out in the end, is extinction a failure?
big_questions.hint: Trilobites lasted about 270 million years. How long has our own species lasted so far?

big_questions.q: You are here partly because an asteroid hit the Earth. What does that tell you about how you came to be?
big_questions.hint: Think about your Empty Board. Did the mammals do anything to earn the empty squares?

big_questions.q: Nobody saw a coelacanth for 66 million years of fossils. When is it fair to say that something is gone?
big_questions.hint: Think about your Last Fossil Test. How many empty layers lay above the last find of the rare kind?

big_questions.q: Life recovered after every mass extinction. So why should people try to prevent one?
big_questions.hint: Compare 10 million years with 300,000 years. Then ask who would be there to see the recovery.

big_questions.q: The asteroid had no choice. People do. Does that make today's extinctions a different kind of event?
big_questions.hint: Think about what could have stopped the asteroid, and what could slow the losses today.

story.title: The Fish Under the Sharks
story.note: This is a true story, told with some imagined details. Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer, Captain Hendrik Goosen, the trawler Nerine, the date, the fish and the colours of the fish, the taxi, the mortuary and the cold store that refused the fish, the taxidermist Robert Center, the letter and sketch to Dr J. L. B. Smith, his telegram, his visit on 16 February 1939 and the name Latimeria chalumnae are all real. The words people say to each other are imagined, except Smith's telegram and his sentence 'There was not a shadow of a doubt', which he wrote later. Marjorie's thoughts, the taxi driver's manner and the last conversation about the rocks are imagined.
text: The telephone rang in the little museum at East London, on the coast of South Africa. It was the twenty-second of December, 1938, and very hot. Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer was thirty-one. She ran the museum almost alone, and she was busy mounting the bones of a fossil reptile before the holiday.
The call was from the docks. Captain Goosen's fishing boat, the Nerine, had come in. He often kept strange fish aside for her. Would she like to look?
She nearly said no. The bones were not finished, and the docks were far. But the crew had been kind to her museum all year, so she went.
On the deck lay a slippery heap of sharks and rays, already drying in the sun. She looked it over and saw nothing she needed. Then, under the heap, she saw one blue fin.

She moved the sharks aside. The fish beneath was as long as she was tall. The scales were as hard as armour. The colour was a pale mauve-blue, flecked with white, with a silver-green shine that moved as she moved. And the fins were wrong. Four of them stood out from the body on thick, fleshy stalks, almost like short legs.
'What is this one?' she asked.
'No idea,' said an old sailor. 'Thirty years at sea, and I never saw one. This fish snapped at the captain's hand.'
She did not know what the fish was either. She only knew that she must not lose this fish.
The taxi driver did not want a dead fish of fifty-seven kilograms on his back seat. She told him she would take another taxi, then. He sighed, and they lifted the fish in together.

At the museum she searched every book she had. No picture matched. The chairman of the museum looked in at the door and said the fish was only a rock cod. She did not think so. A rock cod does not have fins on stalks.

The heat was the enemy now. The museum had no cold room and far too little preserving liquid. She took the fish to the town mortuary, where bodies are kept cold. The man in charge would not have a fish among them. She took the fish to the cold store where the town kept its meat and fruit. They refused as well.

So she went to the one man who could help a little. Mr Center was a taxidermist. His work was to preserve the skins of animals. He wrapped the fish in bedsheets and newspapers soaked in preserving liquid. That would slow the rotting, though it could not stop it.

That evening she wrote to Dr Smith, who knew a great deal about the fishes of South Africa. She could not send him the fish, so she drew a sketch for him. She drew the armoured scales and the strange tail with the extra little tuft at the end. She drew the four fins on their stalks. Then she posted the letter and waited.

No answer came. Dr Smith was far away on holiday, and the letter sat waiting for him. Christmas passed. The fish began to leak oil through the sheets, and the smell grew. On the twenty-seventh, Mr Center told her plainly that the inside could not be saved. If she wanted to keep anything, he must skin the fish now and throw the soft parts away. She said yes, and it felt like losing.
On the third of January a telegram came. MOST IMPORTANT PRESERVE SKELETON AND GILLS. It was a week too late. The gills had gone out with the rubbish.

Dr Smith reached East London on the sixteenth of February. He walked into the room where the stuffed fish stood, and he stopped. He walked all the way round. He touched the scales. When he spoke, his voice was not steady.
'There was not a shadow of a doubt,' he wrote afterwards. He told her the name of the family. Coelacanths.
'I looked in every book,' said Marjorie. 'Why was this fish in none of them?'

'You looked in the books of living fish,' he said. 'These are in the books of fossils. I have seen them only in stone. They were swimming before there were any dinosaurs. The youngest stone one is as old as the last dinosaurs. After that there are no more of them, in any rock, anywhere. Everyone agreed they had died out together with the dinosaurs.'
She looked at the fish, and at the fins on their stalks.
'Then where have they been all this time?'

'Here,' said Dr Smith. 'In deep water, among rocks, where no mud settles to bury a fish and keep the bones for us. They did not stop living. The rocks stopped keeping a record of them, and we took that to mean they were gone.'
Marjorie thought of the heap of sharks, and the one blue fin. She had almost stayed at her desk.
'So one is not enough,' she said. 'We need the gills. We need the inside. We need another fish.'
'We do,' he said. 'And now we know that there is another one to find.'
He named the fish Latimeria, after her. It took fourteen years to find the second one.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the key idea is that having no record of something is different from that thing being gone. Fossil coelacanths stop in rocks about 66 million years old. People read the missing fossils as extinction. But fossils form only where bodies are buried quickly, and the deep rocky slopes where these fish live bury almost nothing. The same idea runs through the Last Fossil Test: the last fossil found is not the last animal. The story also shows a woman without a science degree doing careful science. She noticed what did not fit, refused the easy name of rock cod, and kept the evidence as well as she could.
ask: Why did scientists think coelacanths were extinct?
The fish had been alive all along. So why were there no fossils of them from the last 66 million years?
The chairman said the fish was a rock cod. What did Marjorie see that told her otherwise?
Why was the stuffed skin not enough? What could the gills and the inside have shown?
Can you think of another living being who might be alive now though nobody has seen them for years? How would you search?

games.title: Which Mass Extinction? The clue cards
games.context: This is a card game about the five mass extinctions. Each card gives one clue, and you say which of the five it belongs to.

printables.title: 20 clue cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: This one happened about 444 million years ago. It is the oldest of the five.
items.b: End of the Ordovician. It is the first of the five great extinctions.

items.f: Great ice sheets grew, and the sea level fell.
items.b: End of the Ordovician. Shallow seas drained away, and those seas were where most species lived.

items.f: When this one struck, almost all life was in the sea. There were no forests and no land animals with backbones yet.
items.b: End of the Ordovician. So nearly all the species lost were sea animals.

items.f: The Earth cooled and then warmed again, so sea life was hit twice.
items.b: End of the Ordovician. The cold killed warm-water species, and the warming that followed killed cold-water species.

items.f: This one happened about 370 million years ago.
items.b: Late Devonian. It is the second of the five.

items.f: This one came in several steps, spread over a long time.
items.b: Late Devonian. It was a string of crises and not a single blow.

items.f: One idea for the cause: the first forests changed the air and cooled the Earth.
items.b: Late Devonian. The cause is still argued, and this is one of several ideas.

items.f: Many reef builders and many armoured fishes ended.
items.b: Late Devonian. The warm shallow seas lost the most species.

items.f: This one happened about 252 million years ago. It is the worst of all.
items.b: End of the Permian. About 8 out of 10 sea species ended.

items.f: Huge eruptions in Siberia heated the Earth and made the sea acid.
items.b: End of the Permian. The lava fields are called the Siberian Traps.

items.f: The trilobites ended for ever.
items.b: End of the Permian. Trilobites had lived in the sea for about 270 million years.

items.f: Afterwards, a pig-sized plant-eater named Lystrosaurus was the most common land animal with a backbone. Their fossils lie in the Damodar valley.
items.b: End of the Permian. Lystrosaurus was one of the few land survivors.

items.f: This one happened about 201 million years ago.
items.b: End of the Triassic. It is the fourth of the five.

items.f: The land began to split where the Atlantic Ocean is now, and lava poured out.
items.b: End of the Triassic. Volcanic gases changed the air and the sea.

items.f: Afterwards, dinosaurs became the main large animals on land.
items.b: End of the Triassic. Many of the dinosaurs' large rivals had ended.

items.f: This one comes between the worst extinction and the one with the asteroid.
items.b: End of the Triassic. The order is Ordovician, Devonian, Permian, Triassic, Cretaceous.

items.f: This one happened about 66 million years ago. It is the latest of the five.
items.b: End of the Cretaceous. About 3 out of 4 species ended.

items.f: A thin layer of clay rich in the metal iridium marks it all over the world.
items.b: End of the Cretaceous. Asteroids hold much more iridium than Earth's surface rocks.

items.f: The ammonites and the big dinosaurs ended.
items.b: End of the Cretaceous. Birds, who are small dinosaurs, lived on.

items.f: A crater lies buried in Mexico, and lava of the same age covers much of Maharashtra.
items.b: End of the Cretaceous. The crater is Chicxulub, and the lava is the Deccan Traps.

printables.title: Score sheet
items: One row for each player. Make a mark for every card you keep.

rules: Write the five names on a strip of paper, in order from oldest to latest: Ordovician, Devonian, Permian, Triassic, Cretaceous. Keep it where everyone can see it.
Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, clue side up.
On your turn, read the top card aloud and say which of the five extinctions it belongs to.
Turn the card over. If you were right, keep the card. If not, put the card at the bottom of the pile.
For one extra mark, say one more thing about that extinction.
The game ends when the pile is finished. The player with the most marks wins.
Playing alone: try to keep 16 of the 20 cards on the first time through.

setup.caption: 2. Read the clue. Say which extinction it belongs to.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 20 cards. 2. Write the five names in order on a strip of paper. 3. Shuffle the cards and put them clue side up. 4. Draw a score row for each player.

flow.kid: Cut out the cards and mix them. Write the five names on a strip. Draw a score row.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to read the top card. 2. Say which extinction the clue belongs to. 3. Turn the card over to check. 4. For an extra mark, add one more fact.
flow.say: Read the clue aloud. Which of the five is it? Turn the card over and check. Can you tell me one more thing about that extinction?
flow.kid: Read the clue. Say which extinction it is. Turn the card over to check.

ask.q: Three of the five have volcanoes or lava in their clues. What could lava and gases do to living beings far away?
good: The gases can warm the whole Earth.
They can make the sea acid.
They change the air everywhere, not only near the volcano.

flow.parent: The dates are the easy clues. The causes are harder and matter more. Praise an answer that gives a reason.
flow.context: This is the main part of Which Mass Extinction? Here you read each clue card and say which of the five extinctions it belongs to.

flow.do: 1. Count the marks. 2. Lay the cards in five columns under the strip of names. 3. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Put each card under its name. Look along the five columns. What do the causes have in common?
flow.kid: Count your marks. Put each card under its name. What do the causes share?

check.q: What do the causes of the five mass extinctions have in common?
options: Air, sea or climate changed too fast
check.why: Ice, lava gases and an asteroid are different causes. Each one changed the air, the sea or the climate faster than species could keep up with. If you chose the asteroid, check the cards. Only the last of the five has clear signs of one.

flow.context: This is the last step of Which Mass Extinction? Here you lay the cards under the five names and look for what the causes share.

games.title: Asteroid, Volcanoes or Both? The evidence cards
games.context: This is a card game about what ended the big dinosaurs 66 million years ago. Each card is one piece of real evidence. You decide whether it points to the asteroid, to the Deccan volcanoes, or fits both.

printables.title: 16 evidence cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: A thin clay layer, 66 million years old, holds far more iridium than the rock around it. It is found all over the world.
items.b: Asteroid. Asteroids are rich in iridium. Some volcanoes give out a little iridium too, so this clue alone did not settle the matter.

items.f: The clay layer holds grains of quartz with tiny straight cracks. Only a huge sudden shock makes such cracks.
items.b: Asteroid. Volcanoes do not shock quartz in this way.

items.f: A buried crater 180 to 200 kilometres wide lies in Mexico. It is 66 million years old.
items.b: Asteroid. The crater is called Chicxulub.

items.f: Near the Gulf of Mexico, the layer holds tiny glass beads. They are drops of melted rock that cooled as they flew through the air.
items.b: Asteroid. The strike melted rock and threw it out for thousands of kilometres.

items.f: Lava about 66 million years old covers about 500,000 square kilometres of India.
items.b: Volcanoes. This lava is the Deccan Traps.

items.f: At Anjar in Kutch, layers rich in iridium lie between two lava flows.
items.b: Both. Lava was already flowing before the asteroid's dust settled, and went on flowing after.

items.f: Volcanic gases can warm the whole Earth and make the rain acid.
items.b: Volcanoes. This is a way that eruptions in India could kill species far away.

items.f: Dust and soot high in the air can block sunlight for months, so plants cannot make food.
items.b: Asteroid. A huge strike throws up dust, and the fires it starts make soot.

items.f: A study of old sea temperatures in 2020 found the big sudden change at the time of the strike.
items.b: Asteroid. The eruptions did not line up with the big change in this record.

items.f: Two other mass extinctions, at the end of the Permian and of the Triassic, came at times of huge lava flows. No crater is known for them.
items.b: Volcanoes. Lava floods have gone with mass extinctions before.

items.f: Just above the clay layer, the rock is full of fern spores.
items.b: Both. Ferns are the first plants to cover bare ground. This shows the plants died. It does not show what killed them.

items.f: At a place called Tanis in North America, fossil fish were buried in a rush of water, in rock from the day of the strike.
items.b: Asteroid. It shows sudden death on that day, far from the crater.

items.f: Some kinds of tiny sea fossils seem to fade out in the layers below the clay.
items.b: Volcanoes, with a warning. It may mean trouble before the strike. It may also be the Signor-Lipps effect, where rare fossils seem to stop early.

items.f: Two teams dated the Deccan lava in 2019. They disagreed about whether the biggest flows came before or after the strike.
items.b: Both. This is why the argument is still open.

items.f: In North America, careful searches found dinosaur bones close up to the clay layer.
items.b: Asteroid. It suggests the dinosaurs there lived until the strike and ended suddenly.

items.f: The Deccan eruptions went on for several hundred thousand years, starting before the strike and ending after.
items.b: Both. Life was under strain from the eruptions when the asteroid came.

printables.title: Three heading sheets and a score sheet
items: Write ASTEROID on one sheet of paper, VOLCANOES on a second and BOTH on a third.
One score row for each player. Make a mark for every card you place on the right sheet.

rules: Lay the three heading sheets on the table: ASTEROID, VOLCANOES and BOTH.
Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, evidence side up.
On your turn, read the top card aloud. Say which sheet it belongs on, and give your reason.
Turn the card over. If the back agrees with you, make a mark. Place the card on the sheet the back names.
If you disagree with the back and can give a good reason, the other players may vote to give you the mark.
The game ends when the pile is finished. The player with the most marks wins.
At the end, every player says which cause they think did most of the killing, and names their strongest card.

flow.say: Two huge things happened 66 million years ago. An asteroid struck, and volcanoes poured lava over India. Each card is a real clue. Which one does it point to?

ask.q: Fern spores show that the plants died. Why does that card not tell us who the killer was?
good: Both the asteroid and the volcanoes could have killed the plants.

flow.parent: Giving a reason matters more than matching the back. Some cards can fairly be argued two ways, and scientists argue about them too.

flow.say: Count the three heaps. Which cause do you think did most of the killing? Which one card would you show to someone who disagreed?
flow.kid: Count the three heaps. Say which cause you think did most. Pick your strongest card.

check.q: Most scientists think the asteroid was the main cause. Which fact keeps the argument open?
options: The Deccan lava is hard to date exactly
check.why: The eruptions and the strike happened close together, and two dating methods disagree about the order of the biggest flows. If you chose the crater, it was found in Mexico and its age is known. Iridium is rare in Earth's surface rocks.
