experiments.title: The Empty Board Test: after a mass extinction, who fills the world again?
experiments.question: A paper world of 36 squares is full of species from four groups. A mass extinction wipes out one whole group and about half of the rest. Which group fills the empty squares, and how many rounds does it take?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. The mammals hold 4 squares out of 36 before the extinction. How many will they hold when the board is full again? How many rounds will the refill take? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both runs use the same board, the same starting letters and the same rules. The group D is always wiped out. Every other square has the same chance, one coin toss. Every surviving group rolls the same die once in each round. Only chance differs between the two runs.

materials.item: sheets of plain paper
a pencil, an eraser and a ruler
a coin
a die. If you have none, put six paper chits numbered 1 to 6 in a tumbler and draw one

experiments.record: For each run, draw a table with a row for each round. Write how many squares M, B and R hold, and how many are empty. The four numbers must add up to 36.
experiments.context: In this experiment a grid of 36 squares stands for the world, and each square is one niche. Letters stand for species of four groups. You wipe out most of them with a coin, then refill the board with a die, and count who ends up with the most squares.

setup.art: A hand-drawn grid of 6 by 6 squares on paper, with D written in twenty squares, M in four, B in six and R in six.
setup.caption: 1. Draw 36 squares and fill them with D, M, B and R.

setup.art: The same grid with every D rubbed out, and a child tossing a coin over one of the other squares.
setup.caption: 2. Rub out every D. Toss a coin for each other square. Tails means rub it out.

setup.art: A child rolling a die beside the grid and writing a new M in an empty square next to another M.
setup.caption: 3. Each group rolls the die and adds new squares next to their own.

setup.art: A notebook table with rows for rounds and columns for M, B, R and Empty.
setup.caption: 4. Write the counts after every round, until the board is full.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results for one run

flow.do: 1. Explain that the grid is a world and each square is one niche. 2. Say that M means mammals and holds 4 squares. 3. Ask for the two guesses and the reasons, and write them down.
flow.say: This paper will be a whole world. Soon most of its species will be wiped out. Mammals hold 4 squares now. How many will they hold when the world is full again? How many rounds will that take? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how many squares the mammals will hold at the end. Guess how many rounds it takes. Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think the mammals will hold more squares, fewer, or the same?
good: More, because there will be empty squares to move into.
The same, because they were only 4 to begin with.
It depends on how many of them survive the coin.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children expect the board to go back to what it was before.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Empty Board Test. You guess who will fill a paper world after a mass extinction.

flow.do: 1. Draw a grid of 6 rows and 6 columns, with squares about 3 centimetres wide. 2. In rows 1 to 5, write D in the first four squares. 3. In rows 1 and 2, write M in the last two squares. 4. In rows 3, 4 and 5, write B in the last two squares. 5. Write R in all six squares of row 6. 6. Write lightly in pencil.
flow.say: D stands for big dinosaurs, M for mammals, B for birds and R for the other reptiles. Count each letter. Who holds the most squares?
flow.kid: Draw 6 rows of 6 squares. Write the letters in pencil. Count each letter.
flow.parent: The counts are D 20, M 4, B 6 and R 6. Each letter stands for one species of that group, living in one niche.
flow.context: In this step of the Empty Board Test you draw the full world of 36 squares, before the extinction.

flow.do: 1. Read out the refill rule. A group rolls the die and adds that many new squares. 2. A new square must be empty and must share a side with a square of the same group. 3. Roll once for M, B and R on the full board, and try to follow the rule.
flow.say: Here is the rule for adding a new species. Roll the die. Add that many of your letter, but only in empty squares next to your own. Try it now for the mammals.
flow.kid: Roll the die for M. Try to add new M squares. They must go in empty squares.

check.q: On the full board, the mammals roll a 6. How many new squares can they add?
options: None, because no square is empty
check.why: A new species needs an empty niche, and the full board has none. So the roll changes nothing. If you chose six, look for an empty square to write in. This is a simple picture of why mammals could not spread into the niches of large animals while big dinosaurs held them.

flow.parent: This step is short on purpose. The child should feel that rolling well does not help when there is no room. In the real world a full world still changes slowly. The model leaves that out.
flow.context: In this step of the Empty Board Test you try to add new species to a full board, and find that there is no room.

flow.do: 1. Rub out every D. 2. Go through the other 16 squares one at a time. Toss the coin for each. 3. If the coin shows tails, rub out that letter. 4. Count the M, B and R that are left and the empty squares. Write them in the first row of the table.
flow.say: The asteroid strikes. Every big dinosaur species ends. For each of the others, the coin decides. Heads lives and tails is gone.
flow.kid: Rub out every D. Toss the coin for each other square. Tails means rub it out.
flow.parent: About 8 letters usually survive. Sometimes every M is rubbed out. That is a real result. Keep going, and talk about it at the end.
flow.context: In this step of the Empty Board Test the mass extinction happens. You remove one whole group, and about half of the rest by coin toss.

flow.do: 1. Play a round. M rolls first, then B, then R. 2. A group adds as many squares as the die shows, but never more than the squares the group holds now. 3. Each new square must share a side with a square of that group. 4. After each round, write the four counts. 5. Stop when no square is empty.
flow.say: Now the survivors spread. Roll for each group in turn. A group with 2 squares can add at most 2, even on a roll of 6. Write the counts after every round.
flow.kid: Roll for M, then B, then R. Add new letters next to your own. Write the counts each round.

ask.q: Why can a group with 2 squares add only 2, even if they roll a 6?
good: New species come from the species that are already there.
Two species cannot turn into six all at once.

flow.parent: A group that is walled in by other groups cannot add anything. Say so and move on. The board usually fills in 3 to 6 rounds.
flow.context: This is the main step of the Empty Board Test. The surviving groups roll a die and fill the empty squares round by round.

flow.do: 1. Draw the same starting board on the second sheet. 2. Run the extinction again with the coin. 3. Refill the board with the die, and fill in a second table. 4. Put the two finished boards side by side.
flow.say: Let's run the same world again with the same rules. Do you think the same group will end with the most squares? Why?
flow.kid: Draw the first board again. Do the coin tosses and the rounds again. Compare the two boards.
flow.parent: The second run usually ends differently from the first. That difference is the point of this step.
flow.context: In this step of the Empty Board Test you run the whole test a second time, to see whether the world refills the same way.

flow.do: 1. For the first run, draw a line chart. Put the rounds along the bottom and the number of filled squares up the side. 2. Ask your child what they guessed, what they saw and why it happened. 3. After they have answered, read them the note below.
flow.say: Look at both boards. Say what you guessed, what you saw, and why you think it happened. Did the big dinosaurs ever come back? Did both runs end the same way?
flow.kid: Draw the line chart. Say what you guessed. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Did D ever come back on the board? Why not?
good: No. Every D was gone, so there was none left to make more.
A new species can only come from one that is alive.

ask.q: The mammals had a die on the full board too. What changed for them after the extinction?
good: There were empty squares next to them.
Nothing about the mammals changed. The room around them changed.

flow.parent: In most homes the mammals go from 4 squares to between 8 and 16, and the two runs end differently. Write down what you really got. The reason: a new species needs an empty niche. The full board had none, so no roll could help. The extinction emptied about three quarters of the board, and the survivors had room on every side. The filled squares rise quickly at first and then slowly, because the last empty squares are hard to reach. The lost group never returns, because new species come only from living ones. The model leaves a lot out. Real refilling took about 5 to 10 million years. Real species also change as they spread, so the new mammals were not copies of the old ones.
flow.think: If you ran this world a hundred times, in how many would the mammals end with the most squares?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Empty Board Test. You say what your two runs show about how a world refills after a mass extinction.

experiments.title: The Last Fossil Test: if five species died on the same day, would the rocks show it?
experiments.question: Five species all die out at the same moment, at the top of layer 20 of a paper cliff. Some left many fossils and some left few. When you search the cliff, in which layer is the last fossil of each?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. All five species end at the top of layer 20. In which layer will you find the highest fossil of the commonest species? In which layer for the rarest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All five species lived through every layer and ended at the same moment. You search every layer in the same way, with one roll of the same die. Only one thing differs between the species: how many numbers on the die count as a find.
results_table: Numbers that count as a find

materials.item: a sheet of plain or ruled paper
a pencil, a ruler and a red sketch pen or crayon
a die, or six paper chits numbered 1 to 6 in a tumbler

experiments.record: Draw the cliff as a table with 20 rows and 5 columns. Tick the highest layer where each species is found. For cliffs 2 and 3, write only the layer number of the highest find.
experiments.context: In this experiment a table of 20 rows stands for a cliff of 20 rock layers, with the youngest at the top. Five species all end at the top. You roll a die to search each layer for fossils, and see where the last fossil of each species lies.

setup.art: A table of 20 rows numbered 20 at the top down to 1, with five columns headed A to E and a thick red line drawn across the very top.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a cliff of 20 layers. The red line at the top is the day all five died.

setup.art: Under the column headings, small notes: A finds on 1 to 5, B on 1 to 4, C on 1 to 3, D on 1 or 2, E on 1 only.
setup.caption: 2. Write which rolls count as a find for each species.

setup.art: A child rolling a die and putting a dash in the top row of column E, then moving a finger down to the next row.
setup.caption: 3. Start at layer 20. Roll. No find? Put a dash and go down one layer.

setup.art: The finished table with a tick in each column at a different height, the tick in column E far below the red line.
setup.caption: 4. Tick the first find in each column. That is the last fossil of that species.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: layer of the highest fossil found

flow.do: 1. Explain that the paper will be a cliff of 20 rock layers. 2. Say that five species all die at the very top, on the same day. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason for the commonest and the rarest species. Write them down.
flow.say: Five species all end on the same day, at the top of this cliff. Species A left lots of fossils. Species E left very few. In which layer will you find the last fossil of each? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Five species end on the same day. Guess the layer of the last fossil of each. Say why.

ask.q: Why might the last fossil of E not be in the top layer?
good: E is rare, so there may be no fossil of E in that layer.
You might not find one even if E was alive then.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children say every last fossil will be in layer 20, because that is when the species died.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Last Fossil Test. You guess where in a paper cliff the last fossils of five species will be found.

flow.do: 1. Draw a table with 20 rows and 5 columns. 2. Number the rows from 20 at the top to 1 at the bottom. 3. Head the columns A, B, C, D and E. 4. Draw a thick red line across the top. 5. Under each heading, write the rolls that count as a find.
flow.say: The top row is the youngest rock. A is found on a roll of 1 to 5. B on 1 to 4. C on 1 to 3. D on 1 or 2. E only on a 1.
flow.kid: Draw 20 rows and 5 columns. Number them from 20 at the top. Draw a red line on top.
flow.parent: Every species was alive in every layer. The die only decides whether a fossil of that species was made, kept and found in that layer.
flow.context: In this step of the Last Fossil Test you draw the paper cliff and write the finding rule for each of the five species.

flow.do: 1. Begin with species A in layer 20. Roll the die. 2. If the roll counts as a find, put a tick and stop searching for A. 3. If not, put a dash and go down one layer. Roll again. 4. Do the same for B, C, D and E. 5. If you reach layer 1 with no find, write 'none found'.
flow.say: We only want the highest fossil of each species, so stop at the first tick. Start at the top each time and work down.
flow.kid: Start at layer 20. Roll. A find gets a tick. No find gets a dash. Then go down.

check.q: In your cliff, species E has dashes in layers 20 to 15 and a tick in layer 14. When did E really die out?
options: At the top of layer 20, with the others
check.why: In this test every species ends at the top of layer 20. The dashes are layers where E was alive and no fossil was found. If you chose layer 14, that is what the cliff seems to say, and it is what a fossil hunter might conclude.

flow.parent: Species A is usually ticked in layer 20. Species E is often ticked five or more layers lower. About 1 time in 40, E is not found at all.
flow.context: In this step of the Last Fossil Test you search the cliff from the top down with a die, and mark the highest fossil of each species.

flow.do: 1. Search a second cliff in the same way. You need not draw it. Count down the layers aloud as you roll. 2. Write only the layer of the highest find for each species. 3. Do the same for a third cliff.
flow.say: One cliff can be a fluke. Let's search two more cliffs. Count down from 20 as you roll, and write the layer of the first find.
flow.kid: Search two more cliffs. Count down from 20 as you roll. Write the layer of each first find.
flow.parent: Three cliffs show the pattern better than one. In a single cliff, E can be found in layer 20 by luck.
flow.context: In this step of the Last Fossil Test you search two more paper cliffs, because one result can be a fluke.

flow.do: 1. For cliff 1, draw a bar for each species. The height of the bar is the layer of the highest find. 2. Draw the red line across the chart at 20. 3. For each species, find the highest find in any of the three cliffs. Write it beside the bar.
flow.say: Draw a bar up to the last fossil of each species. Then look at all three cliffs together. What is the highest layer for each?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each species. Draw the red line at 20. Find the best of three cliffs.
flow.parent: The bars for cliff 1 usually step down from A to E. The best of three cliffs is usually much closer to 20 for every species.
flow.context: In this step of the Last Fossil Test you draw a bar chart of where the last fossil of each species was found.

flow.do: 1. Cover the red line with a ruler. 2. Ask what a fossil hunter who saw only cliff 1 would say about how these species ended. 3. Ask your child what they guessed, what they saw and why it happened. 4. Then read the note below.
flow.say: Suppose you found only this cliff and knew nothing else. Would you say the five species ended together, or one after another? Now tell me what you guessed, what you saw, and why.
flow.kid: Hide the red line. Do the species seem to end together? Say what you saw and why.

ask.q: All five ended on the same day. Why does the cliff make it look slow?
good: The rare ones were not found in the top layers.
No fossil found does not mean none was alive.

ask.q: How did searching three cliffs change the picture?
good: The highest finds moved up towards layer 20.
More searching makes the gap smaller.

flow.parent: The reason: a rare species leaves few fossils, so there are many layers where they lived and nothing was found. Their last fossil lies below their real end. Common species leave a fossil in nearly every layer, so their last fossil lies close to the real end. A sudden ending therefore looks like a slow one. Scientists call this the Signor-Lipps effect. The cure is more searching. The same thinking explains how a fish could be missing from 66 million years of rock and still be alive.
flow.think: Is the first fossil of a species the first animal of that species? What would the die say?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Last Fossil Test. You say what your cliffs show about reading the end of a species from fossils.

activities.title: The Hundred Squares: how many of all the species that ever lived are alive today?
activities.context: In this activity a grid of 100 squares stands for every species that has ever lived. You guess how many squares stand for the species alive today, and then find out. It opens the main question of the unit: where did all the others go?

materials.item: a page from a squared maths notebook, or plain paper and a ruler
a pencil and one colour pencil

activities.record: Keep the grid. Write your guess beside it, and the estimate scientists give.

setup.art: A grid of 10 by 10 squares drawn on squared paper, with a pencil beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Mark out 100 squares. They stand for every species that ever lived.

setup.art: The grid with about thirty squares lightly shaded in pencil and a question mark beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Shade your guess: how many are alive today?

setup.art: The same grid with only one square coloured brightly in a corner.
setup.caption: 3. Colour the scientists' estimate. It is fewer than one square.

flow.do: 1. Mark out a block of 10 rows and 10 columns on squared paper. 2. Say that the 100 squares stand for every species that ever lived on Earth. 3. Ask how many squares stand for the species alive today, and why. 4. Shade the guess lightly in pencil.
flow.say: These 100 squares are every species that ever lived, from the first cells until now. How many squares do you think are alive today? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Mark out 100 squares. Guess how many stand for species alive today. Shade your guess lightly.

ask.q: Why did you choose that number?
good: I think most are alive, because there are so many animals and plants.
I think only some, because dinosaurs and many others are gone.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most children and most adults guess between 20 and 80.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Hundred Squares. You guess how many of all the species that ever lived are alive today.

flow.do: 1. Say that scientists estimate fewer than 1 in 100. 2. Colour one square brightly. 3. Rub out the pencil shading on the others. 4. Ask what happened to the other 99.
flow.say: Scientists estimate that fewer than one square is alive today. Colour just one. What do you think happened to the species in the other ninety-nine?
flow.kid: Colour only one square. That is all the species alive today. What happened to the rest?

ask.q: Does this mean there were once 100 times more species alive than now?
good: No. They did not all live at the same time.
Species kept ending and new ones kept starting.

flow.parent: The number is an estimate. Most species left no fossils, so nobody can count them. The point to reach is that the 99 squares were never alive together. Species come and go like people in a town over a thousand years.
flow.context: In this step of the Hundred Squares you colour the scientists' estimate, which is fewer than one square in a hundred.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to write one question that the grid makes them wonder about. 2. Ask the question below. 3. Keep the grid for the end of the unit.
flow.say: Write down one thing this grid makes you wonder. Here is my question. If nearly every species ends, why is the world still full of life?
flow.kid: Write one thing you wonder about. Then think: why is the world still full of life?

check.q: Nearly every species that ever lived is extinct. Why is the Earth still full of species?
options: New species keep arising from living ones
No species has ended for a long time
check.why: While some species end, others split into new species, so the total stays high. If you chose that extinct species come back, they never do. Their relatives may live on, as birds do for the dinosaurs.

flow.parent: Good questions to hear: Did they all die at once? Who was the first? Will we end too? The unit takes up each of these.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Hundred Squares. You ask why the world is still full of life if nearly every species ends.

activities.title: Five Marks on a Paper Road: a time line of the mass extinctions
activities.context: In this activity you make a paper strip on which 1 centimetre stands for 10 million years. You mark the five mass extinctions on it, and draw the lives of four groups of animals across them.

materials.item: a sheet of A4 paper, cut into long strips about 5 centimetres wide
sticky tape or glue
a ruler of 30 centimetres, a pencil, a red pen and a blue pen
scissors

activities.safety: A grown-up helps with the scissors if needed.
activities.record: Keep the strip. Write the scale on it: 1 centimetre is 10 million years.

setup.art: Two long paper strips taped end to end on a floor, with a ruler lying along them.
setup.caption: 1. Tape two strips into one strip at least 55 centimetres long.

setup.art: The strip with the right end labelled 'now' and five red lines drawn across it at uneven gaps.
setup.caption: 2. Measure back from 'now' and draw five red lines.

setup.art: The same strip with four blue bars of different lengths drawn along it, some stopping at a red line.
setup.caption: 3. Draw a blue bar for each group, from their start to their end.

flow.do: 1. Cut two strips from the long side of the A4 sheet. 2. Tape them end to end. 3. Write 'now' at the right end. 4. Write the scale on the strip: 1 centimetre is 10 million years.
flow.say: This strip is a road back in time. Each centimetre is 10 million years. How far back does one finger-width take us?
flow.kid: Tape two strips into one long strip. Write 'now' at the right end. Write the scale.
flow.parent: One finger-width is about 1 centimetre, so 10 million years. The strip covers about 550 million years, the time from which fossils of animals are common.
flow.context: This is the first step of Five Marks on a Paper Road. You make the strip and set its scale.

flow.do: 1. Measure back from 'now' and draw a red line at each distance. 2. The distances are 6.6, 20.1, 25.2, 37 and 44.4 centimetres. 3. Label the lines Cretaceous, Triassic, Permian, Devonian and Ordovician, in that order.
flow.say: The asteroid came 66 million years ago. How many centimetres is that? Measure it and draw a red line. Now the other four.
flow.kid: Measure back from 'now'. Draw the five red lines. Use the distances in the list.

check.q: On a strip where 1 centimetre is 10 million years, how far from 'now' is 252 million years ago?
check.why: 252 divided by 10 is 25.2. If you chose 252, that would be one centimetre for each million years. Here one centimetre holds ten million years.

flow.parent: Ask your child to work out each distance by dividing the millions of years by 10, before you read the list.
flow.context: In this step of Five Marks on a Paper Road you measure and mark the five mass extinctions on the strip.

flow.do: 1. Draw a blue bar for trilobites from 52 centimetres to 25.2 centimetres. 2. Draw a bar for ammonites from 41 to 6.6. 3. Draw a bar for big dinosaurs from 23 to 6.6. 4. Draw a bar for mammals from 22.5 to 'now'. 5. Make a dot for our own species at 0.3 millimetres from 'now'.
flow.say: Each blue bar is the whole life of one group. Start where the group begins and stop where the group ends. Which bars stop at a red line?
flow.kid: Draw the four blue bars. Start and stop where the list says. Look where each bar ends.
flow.parent: Our own species is about 300,000 years old. On this scale that is three tenths of a millimetre, thinner than the pencil line.
flow.context: In this step of Five Marks on a Paper Road you draw the lives of trilobites, ammonites, big dinosaurs and mammals across the strip.

flow.do: 1. Look at the strip together. 2. Ask what your child notices about the gaps between the red lines. 3. Ask which groups crossed a red line and which stopped at one.
flow.say: What do you notice about the gaps between the red lines? Which group crossed two red lines and stopped at the third?
flow.kid: Look at the gaps between the red lines. Which bar crosses two lines and stops at the third?

ask.q: The mammals' bar starts before the dinosaurs' bar ends. What does that tell you?
good: Mammals lived at the same time as the big dinosaurs.
Mammals did not appear after the dinosaurs. They were already there.

flow.parent: Things to notice: the gaps are uneven, so extinctions do not come on a timetable. Trilobites crossed two red lines. Ammonites crossed three. Mammals and big dinosaurs began at almost the same time.
flow.context: This is the last step of Five Marks on a Paper Road. You read the finished strip and say what you notice.

activities.title: Three Rules for Survival: test them against thirteen real cases
activities.context: In this activity you test three possible rules for who lived through the asteroid strike of 66 million years ago. You try each rule on thirteen real groups of animals and count how often the rule is right.

materials.item: a sheet of paper, a pencil and a ruler

activities.record: Keep the table. Under it, write how many of the thirteen cases each rule got right.

setup.art: A table on paper with thirteen rows lettered A to M and four columns headed Rule 1, Rule 2, Rule 3 and What happened.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a table with thirteen rows and four columns.

setup.art: A child writing L or E in the first three columns of one row while reading a short description.
setup.caption: 2. For each case, write what each rule says: L for lived, E for ended.

setup.art: The finished table with the last column filled in and ticks and crosses beside each rule's guesses.
setup.caption: 3. Fill in what really happened. Tick each right guess and count.

flow.do: 1. Draw a table with 13 rows, lettered A to M. 2. Make four columns: Rule 1, Rule 2, Rule 3, and What happened. 3. Read the three rules aloud. Rule 1: animals under 25 kilograms lived. Rule 2: animals whose food chain began with dead matter or seeds lived. Rule 3: animals with a shelter lived. 4. Ask which rule your child expects to work best, and why.
flow.say: Scientists ask why some groups lived and others ended. Here are three possible rules. Which one do you think will be right most often? Why?
flow.kid: Draw the table. Rule 1: small ones lived. Rule 2: eaters of dead matter or seeds lived. Rule 3: ones with shelter lived. Guess the best rule.
flow.parent: A shelter here means a burrow, mud, or water in a river, a lake or the deep sea. Food chains that begin with living leaves or with floating algae count as 'fresh food'.
flow.context: This is the first step of Three Rules for Survival. You set up a table and guess which of three rules explains best who survived the asteroid strike.

flow.do: 1. Read cases A to G. For each, write L or E under each rule. 2. A. Tyrannosaurus: heavier than an elephant, ate plant-eaters, no shelter. 3. B. Triceratops: heavier than an elephant, ate living plants, no shelter. 4. C. A titanosaur of India: as heavy as several elephants, ate living plants, no shelter. 5. D. A shrew-sized mammal: ate insects and worms from the leaf litter, lived in a burrow. 6. E. A ground bird the size of a quail: ate seeds and insects, hid in holes and marshes. 7. F. A small toothed bird of the treetops: ate insects, nested in trees. 8. G. A river crocodile: far over 25 kilograms, ate fish and dead animals, lived in water.
flow.say: Take one case at a time. What does Rule 1 say, lived or ended? What does Rule 2 say? And Rule 3? Write L or E for each.
flow.kid: A: Tyrannosaurus, huge, ate plant-eaters, no shelter. B: Triceratops, huge, ate plants, no shelter. C: titanosaur, huge, ate plants, no shelter. D: tiny mammal, ate insects, had a burrow. E: small ground bird, ate seeds, hid in holes. F: small tree bird, ate insects, no shelter. G: big crocodile, ate fish and dead animals, lived in water. Write L or E for each rule.
flow.parent: Insects and worms of the leaf litter feed on dead matter, so D, E and F count as 'dead matter or seeds' under Rule 2. The forests burned or died, so a tree nest counts as no shelter.
flow.context: This step of Three Rules for Survival is the first half of the cases. You write what each rule says about cases A to G.

flow.do: 1. Read cases H to M in the same way. 2. H. A river turtle: a few kilograms, ate water plants and dead matter, lived in water and mud. 3. I. A mosasaur, a sea lizard as long as a bus: ate fish and ammonites in the open sea, no shelter. 4. J. An ammonite: small, the young floated among tiny algae in the open sea, no shelter. 5. K. A nautilus: small, ate dead animals, lived in deep water. 6. L. A frog: small, ate insects, lived in ponds and mud. 7. M. Pouched mammals of North America: small, ate insects, lived in burrows.
flow.say: Now cases H to M. Remember that the open sea near the surface is no shelter. Its food chain begins with floating algae, which need light.
flow.kid: H: river turtle, small, lived in water and mud. I: mosasaur, huge, hunted in the open sea. J: ammonite, small, young floated among algae. K: nautilus, small, ate dead animals, deep water. L: frog, small, ate insects, lived in mud. M: small pouched mammals, ate insects, had burrows. Write L or E for each rule.
flow.parent: All three rules say L for case M. That case is there for a reason, which the next step shows.
flow.context: This step of Three Rules for Survival is the second half of the cases. You write what each rule says about cases H to M.

flow.do: 1. Fill in the last column. Lived: D, E, G, H, K and L. Ended: A, B, C, F, I and J. For M, write 'most species ended'. 2. Tick every guess that matches. 3. Count the ticks for each rule, out of 13. 4. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Here is what really happened. Tick each guess that was right, and count the ticks for each rule. Did any rule get all thirteen right?
flow.kid: Fill in what really happened. Tick the right guesses. Count the ticks for each rule.

ask.q: Which cases did Rule 1 get wrong? What does that tell you about size?
good: The crocodile was big and lived. The tree bird and the ammonite were small and ended.
Size mattered, but size alone does not explain it.

ask.q: All three rules said the pouched mammals would live, and most of their species ended. What else might matter?
good: Luck.
Where they lived. North America was close to the strike.
Something we have not thought of yet.

flow.parent: The counts should be 9 for Rule 1, 11 for Rule 2 and 12 for Rule 3. No rule gets 13. These thirteen cases were chosen to be clear, and the full record is messier. Scientists think size, food and shelter all mattered, and that luck did too. A good answer notices that before the strike none of these features looked special.

check.q: Great size helped dinosaurs for millions of years. Why did it harm them after the asteroid strike?
options: A big body needs a lot of food every day
The asteroid aimed at big animals
check.why: With the plants dead, there was almost no food, and a large animal starves first. If you chose 'slower', speed was not the problem. No animal could outrun months without food.

flow.context: This is the last step of Three Rules for Survival. You compare each rule's guesses with what really happened and count how often each rule was right.

activities.title: Gone, Gone From Here, or Found Again? Seven case files
activities.context: In this activity you sort seven real species into four groups: extinct everywhere, gone from one country, found again, and alive but at risk. Then you ask how anyone can be sure that a species is gone.

materials.item: a sheet of paper and a pencil

activities.record: Keep the sheet with the four headings and the letters of the cases under them.

setup.art: A sheet of paper divided into four boxes headed Extinct everywhere, Gone from one country, Found again, and Alive but at risk.
setup.caption: 1. Draw four boxes and write the four headings.

setup.art: A child writing a letter in one of the boxes while a parent reads from a phone.
setup.caption: 2. Listen to each case. Write the letter in the box that fits.

flow.do: 1. Draw four boxes on the paper. 2. Write the headings: Extinct everywhere, Gone from one country, Found again, and Alive but at risk. 3. Explain that a species is called extinct only when careful searches leave no reasonable doubt.
flow.say: People say 'extinct' quickly. Scientists are careful with the word. Let's sort seven real species into these four boxes.
flow.kid: Draw four boxes. Write the four headings. Get ready to sort seven species.
flow.context: This is the first step of Gone, Gone From Here, or Found Again? You set up four boxes for sorting seven real species.

flow.do: 1. Read each case and write the letter in the box that fits. 2. A. The dodo of Mauritius: last surely seen in 1662. 3. B. The cheetah in India: declared gone in 1952, still living in Africa. 4. C. The coelacanth: known only from fossils until a fresh one was caught in 1938. 5. D. Jerdon's courser of Andhra Pradesh: no record from 1900 until one was caught in 1986. 6. E. The passenger pigeon: the last one died in a zoo in 1914. 7. F. The tiger: a few thousand live wild in India. 8. G. The slender-billed curlew: a bird declared extinct in 2025 after many years of searching.
flow.say: Listen to each case. Which box does it belong in? Tell me what makes you sure.
flow.kid: A: dodo, last seen 1662. B: cheetah in India, gone in 1952, alive in Africa. C: coelacanth, a fossil fish caught alive in 1938. D: Jerdon's courser, missing 1900 to 1986. E: passenger pigeon, last one died 1914. F: tiger, a few thousand left. G: slender-billed curlew, declared extinct in 2025. Sort them.
flow.parent: Answers. Extinct everywhere: A, E and G. Gone from one country: B. Found again: C and D. Alive but at risk: F. In September 2022, eight cheetahs from Namibia were brought to Kuno National Park in Madhya Pradesh. They are African cheetahs, so the cheetahs that India lost have not come back.
flow.context: This is the main step of Gone, Gone From Here, or Found Again? You sort seven real species into the four boxes.

flow.do: 1. Look at the two cases in the 'Found again' box. 2. Ask why each was missed for so long. 3. Ask the question below.
flow.say: The courser was missed for 86 years. The coelacanth was missed for far longer. Why were they so hard to find? When is it fair to say a species is gone?
flow.kid: Look at the 'Found again' box. Why were those two missed for so long? When is 'gone' fair?

ask.q: Why is it easier to be sure about the dodo than about the courser?
good: The dodo was big, could not fly and lived on one small island.
The courser is small, comes out at night and lives in thick scrub.

check.q: Nobody has seen a small night bird in a thick forest for 30 years. What is the fairest thing to say?
options: Not found yet, so search carefully
check.why: A small night bird is easy to miss, so 30 years without a sighting is weak evidence. If you chose 'certainly extinct', remember Jerdon's courser, missed for 86 years. Being sure they live is also a guess.

flow.parent: A species found again is nearly always very rare. Finding one is the start of the work to protect them.
flow.context: This is the last step of Gone, Gone From Here, or Found Again? You ask how anyone can be sure that a species is extinct.

activities.title: Fifty Times Faster: work out today's extinction rate on squared paper
activities.context: In this activity you compare two numbers on squared paper. One is how many species of animals with backbones should have ended since 1900 at the normal rate. The other is how many really did.

materials.item: a page from a squared maths notebook
a pencil and two colour pencils

activities.record: Keep the page with the two coloured blocks. Write your two answers under it.

setup.art: A squared notebook page with a small block of 9 squares coloured green in one corner.
setup.caption: 1. Colour 9 squares. That is the normal number of losses since 1900.

setup.art: The same page with a large block of 477 squares coloured red beside the small green block.
setup.caption: 2. Colour 477 squares. That is the cautious count of real losses.

setup.art: A child writing a division sum under the two coloured blocks.
setup.caption: 3. Work out how many times bigger the red block is.

flow.do: 1. Give the normal rate: 2 species lost out of every 10,000, in 100 years. 2. Say that scientists have checked about 40,000 species of animals with backbones. 3. Ask how many of these should end in 100 years at the normal rate. 4. Colour that many squares green, and one more.
flow.say: In normal times, 2 species out of 10,000 end in 100 years. There are about 40,000 species of animals with backbones. How many should end in 100 years?
flow.kid: The normal rate is 2 in 10,000 each 100 years. Work it out for 40,000 species. Colour your answer green.
flow.parent: 40,000 is 4 lots of 10,000, so 4 times 2 is 8 species in 100 years. The time since 1900 is a little over 100 years, so the study expected about 9. Colour 9 squares.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fifty Times Faster. You work out how many species of animals with backbones should have ended since 1900 at the normal rate.

flow.do: 1. Say that on a cautious count, 477 such species are gone or very probably gone since 1900. 2. Ask for a guess: how big will a block of 477 squares be? 3. Colour 477 squares red. A quick way is 4 rows of 100, then 77 more.
flow.say: The real number is 477. Before you colour it, show me with your hands how big you think the red block will be. Now colour it.
flow.kid: The real number is 477. Guess how big that block is. Colour 477 squares red.
flow.parent: If the page is too small, let each square stand for 3 species. Then colour 3 green squares and 159 red ones.
flow.context: In this step of Fifty Times Faster you colour the number of species of animals with backbones really lost since 1900.

flow.do: 1. Ask how many times bigger the red block is than the green one. 2. Ask how long 477 losses would take at the normal rate of 8 in 100 years. 3. Ask what fraction of 40,000 is 477. 4. After your child has answered, read the note below.
flow.say: How many times bigger is the red block? At 8 losses in each 100 years, how long would 477 losses take? Is 477 a large part of 40,000?
flow.kid: How many times bigger is red than green? How long would 477 take at 8 each 100 years?

ask.q: The losses are 50 times the normal number, and yet most species are still here. How can both be true?
good: 477 is only about 1 in 84 of the 40,000 species.
The rate is very high, but it has not been going on for long.

check.q: Losses since 1900 are about 53 times the normal number. What does that mean?
options: Species are ending much faster than normal
check.why: The 53 compares two rates: 477 real losses against 9 expected. If you chose 53 out of 100, look at your page. The red block is about 1 part in 84 of all the species checked.

flow.parent: 477 divided by 9 is 53. At 8 in each 100 years, 477 losses would take about 60 lots of 100 years, which is 6,000 years. 477 out of 40,000 is about 1 in 84. So the rate is far above normal, and most species are still alive. Both facts matter. A mass extinction means about 3 in 4 gone. That is why some scientists say one has begun, and others say it can still be prevented.
flow.context: This is the last step of Fifty Times Faster. You compare the real losses with the normal number, and work out what the difference means.

projects.title: The Dark Week: who gets through a time without sunlight?
projects.context: In this eight-day project you sprout moong seeds and then keep some seedlings in the dark, some in the light, and some dry seeds in the dark. It is a small model of the dark months after the asteroid strike, when plants could not make food.

materials.item: whole green moong seeds
small steel plates or bowls
pieces of clean cotton cloth, each about the size of a handkerchief
a cardboard box with a lid, such as a shoe box
a paper envelope or a twist of newspaper for the dry seeds
a ruler, a notebook and a pencil

projects.safety: Do not eat the seedlings from this test. Throw them away if you see fuzzy mould or notice a bad smell.

schedule.what: Soak 40 moong seeds in water overnight. Put 20 dry seeds in a paper envelope inside the box.
Spread the soaked seeds on two damp cloths, 20 on each plate. Keep both plates in the light.
Both plates have sprouted. Guess what will happen. Put plate B in the closed box. Leave plate A near a window.
Sprinkle water on both cloths. Close the box again quickly.
Sprinkle water on both cloths. Close the box again quickly.
Compare the two plates. Measure five seedlings from each. End the dark time: put plate B in the light, and wet the 20 dry seeds on the third cloth.
Look at all three plates. Say who got through the dark time, and how.

projects.record: A notebook page with your guess, a table of the heights and colours on day 6, and two drawings: one seedling from the light and one from the dark.

setup.art: Two steel plates of sprouted moong on damp cloth, one on a window sill and one being placed into a shoe box, with a small paper envelope of dry seeds already in the box.
setup.caption: 1. One plate stays in the light. One plate and the dry seeds go into the dark box.

setup.art: After three days: short green seedlings with open leaves on the window plate, and tall, thin, pale yellow seedlings leaning over on the box plate.
setup.caption: 2. After three days in the dark, compare height, colour and leaves.

setup.art: A third plate where the dry seeds from the box have just sprouted on a damp cloth, beside the two older plates.
setup.caption: 3. Wet the dry seeds. Two days later, see who has come through.

flow.do: 1. Count 60 moong seeds. 2. Put 40 in a bowl of water to soak overnight. 3. Put the other 20, dry, in a paper envelope inside the box. 4. Explain that the box will stand for the dark months after the asteroid strike.
flow.say: After the asteroid, dust and soot hid the Sun for months. We will make a small dark time in this box. These twenty seeds will wait in it, dry.
flow.kid: Soak 40 moong seeds in water. Put 20 dry seeds in an envelope in the box.
flow.parent: Use whole green moong, the kind sold for sprouting. Split dal will not grow.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Dark Week. You soak moong seeds and set aside dry seeds, to model the dark months after the asteroid strike.

flow.do: 1. Wet two cloths and squeeze them so they are damp, not dripping. 2. Lay one on each plate. 3. Spread 20 soaked seeds on each. 4. Label the plates A and B. Keep both in a bright place, out of hot sun.
flow.say: Both plates get the same seeds, the same water and the same light for one day. Why should we start them the same way?
flow.kid: Put 20 soaked seeds on each damp cloth. Label the plates A and B. Keep both in the light.
flow.parent: Starting both the same way makes the test fair. The only difference later will be light.
flow.wait: Leave both plates in the light until the next day.
flow.context: This is day 2 of the Dark Week. You start two plates of moong seeds in exactly the same way.

flow.do: 1. Check that both plates have sprouted. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason for all three groups: the seedlings in light, the seedlings in the dark and the dry seeds. 3. Write the guesses down. 4. Put plate B in the box and close the lid. Leave plate A near a window.
flow.say: Plate B goes into the dark for three days. What will these seedlings look like on day 6? What about the dry seeds? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess what each group will look like on day 6. Say why. Put plate B in the box.

ask.q: A seedling has no leaves in the sun yet. Where is the food coming from to grow?
good: From the seed.
The seed has a store of food packed inside.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Many children say the dark seedlings will stay short or will die at once.
flow.wait: Leave the plates for three days. Sprinkle water on both each day.
flow.context: This is day 3 of the Dark Week. You guess what three days of darkness will do, and put one plate in the dark box.

flow.do: 1. On day 4 and on day 5, open the box for a few seconds. 2. Sprinkle a spoon of water on each cloth. 3. Close the lid again at once.
flow.say: A few seconds of light will not spoil the test. Sprinkle the same water on both plates.
flow.kid: Each day, sprinkle a spoon of water on both cloths. Close the box quickly.
flow.parent: Keep the cloths damp, not flooded. Standing water brings mould. If you see fuzzy mould, throw that plate away and start again with less water.
flow.context: These are days 4 and 5 of the Dark Week. You keep both plates of seedlings damp and keep plate B in the dark.

flow.do: 1. On day 6, put the two plates side by side. 2. Measure the height of five seedlings from each plate. Write the colour and whether the leaves have opened. 3. Ask what your child guessed, what they see and why. 4. Put plate B in the light. 5. Spread the 20 dry seeds on the third damp cloth.
flow.say: Look closely at both plates. What is different? Say what you guessed, what you see, and why you think it happened. The dark time is over now.
flow.kid: Measure five seedlings from each plate. Write their colour. Then put plate B in the light. Wet the dry seeds.

ask.q: The dark seedlings are taller. Does that mean the dark was good for them?
good: No. They are thin and yellow and they fall over.
They used up their food reaching for light they did not find.

flow.parent: Expect the seedlings in the dark to be about twice as tall, thin, pale yellow, with small closed leaves. Many will be leaning over. The seedlings in the light are shorter, sturdy and green. The reason: a seedling in the dark spends the seed's food store on growing upwards, towards where light should be. A seedling in the dark makes no chlorophyll, the green substance that catches light, so no new food is made. When the store is gone, the seedling dies. Three days is short enough for most to live.
flow.wait: Leave all three plates in the light for two days. Keep the cloths damp.
flow.context: This is day 6 of the Dark Week. You compare seedlings kept in the dark with seedlings kept in the light, and then end the dark time.

flow.do: 1. On day 8, look at all three plates. 2. Ask which group came through the dark time with no harm at all. 3. Ask what would have happened to plate B after three months of dark.
flow.say: Look at the dry seeds now. Look at the pale seedlings. Who came through the dark time best? What if the dark had lasted for months?
flow.kid: Look at all three plates. Who came through the dark best? What if the dark lasted months?

ask.q: After the asteroid strike, the dark lasted for months. Which plants could come back?
good: The ones waiting as seeds or spores in the soil.
Not the ones that were already growing.

check.q: Sunlight is blocked for many months. Which has the best chance of growing afterwards?
options: A dry seed lying in the soil
check.why: A dry seed uses almost none of the stored food while waiting. A seedling or a leafy tree must keep making food and cannot, so the store runs out. If you chose the tree, a few trees can regrow from roots, but most growing plants died.

flow.parent: Most of the dry seeds should have sprouted, as if nothing had happened. The pale seedlings should be turning green. This is why the first plants after the strike grew from spores and seeds, and why animals who could eat seeds had food.
flow.context: This is day 8, the last day of the Dark Week. You see which group came through the dark time, and what that says about the months after the asteroid strike.

challenges.title: The Thirty-Roll Search: plan a fossil hunt that gets closest to the truth
challenges.context: This is a planning challenge. In the Last Fossil Test, the last fossils of rare species lay far below the layer where they really ended. Here you have only 30 rolls of the die, and you plan how to spend them so that your cliff tells the truth as nearly as it can.
challenges.problem: Five species, A to E, all end at the top of layer 20. You may roll the die only 30 times in all. Plan your search so that the last fossil you find of each species is as close to layer 20 as possible.
constraints: Each roll searches one layer for one species. You choose the species and the layer before you roll.
The finding rules are those of the Last Fossil Test. A is found on 1 to 5, B on 1 to 4, C on 1 to 3, D on 1 or 2, and E only on 1.
You may search the same layer again for the same species. Each new search costs one roll. It stands for digging more rock from that layer.
Your score is the total of the five gaps. A gap is 20 minus the highest layer where you found that species. A species never found scores a gap of 20. The lowest score is best.
materials: a die, or six paper chits numbered 1 to 6 in a tumbler
paper, a pencil and a ruler
your results from the Last Fossil Test, if you have them
general: Share the rolls equally: 6 for each species, working down from layer 20, one roll for each layer.
Give the common species fewer rolls and the rare species more, still working down one layer at a time.
Stop searching for a species as soon as you find one fossil, and pass the spare rolls to the next species.
creative: Search layer 20 again and again for the rare species, and move down only if you run short of rolls.
Search the rare species first, while you still have all your rolls, and leave the common ones for last.
Keep back five rolls for a last try at layer 20 for the species with the biggest gap.
challenges.your_turn: Now make your own plan for 30 rolls. Write it down before you roll. Run it and work out your score. Then explain to someone why your plan gave a smaller total gap than sharing the rolls equally, or why it did not.

setup.art: A notebook page headed '30 rolls' with a plan written as a small table: species A to E and the number of rolls for each.
setup.caption: 1. Write your plan: which species and which layer each roll will search.

setup.art: A child rolling a die and making a tally mark for each roll used, beside a paper cliff of 20 layers.
setup.caption: 2. Roll, tally each roll, and tick each fossil you find.

setup.art: Two score lines on the page, one labelled 'equal plan' and one labelled 'my plan', with the total gap under each.
setup.caption: 3. Add up the five gaps for each plan and compare.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem and the four rules aloud. 2. Work out one gap together as an example. A highest find in layer 14 gives a gap of 6. 3. Draw a cliff table with 20 rows and 5 columns.
flow.say: You have only 30 rolls for the whole cliff. The score is the total of the five gaps, and the lowest score wins. What is the gap if the highest find is in layer 14?
flow.kid: Read the rules. You have 30 rolls. A gap is 20 minus your highest find. Draw the cliff.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Thirty-Roll Search. You learn the rules of a fossil hunt that is limited to 30 rolls of the die.

flow.do: 1. Try the equal plan first. Give each species 6 rolls. 2. For each species, search layers 20, 19, 18, 17, 16 and 15, one roll each. Stop at the first find. 3. Write the five gaps and add them up.
flow.say: Let's try the plain plan first. Six rolls for each species, one layer at a time from the top. What is your total gap?
flow.kid: Give each species 6 rolls, from layer 20 down. Stop at a find. Add up the five gaps.
flow.parent: With this plan, species E is not found at all about one time in three, which costs a gap of 20. A total between 3 and 25 is usual.
flow.context: In this step of the Thirty-Roll Search you try the simplest plan, sharing the 30 rolls equally among the five species.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to design a better plan and write it down. 2. Ask why they expect the plan to work. 3. Run the plan with exactly 30 rolls or fewer. 4. Write the five gaps and the total.
flow.say: Now design your own plan. Where were the rolls wasted last time? Where were there too few? Write the plan, tell me why, and then roll.
flow.kid: Make your own plan for 30 rolls. Write it down and say why. Then roll and score.

ask.q: Which species needs the most rolls, and why?
good: E, because E is found only on a 1.
The rare ones, because each search is less likely to find them.

flow.parent: Let your child find the strong idea alone if possible. It is to search layer 20 many times for the rare species. Spare rolls come from the common species, who are usually found in one or two rolls.
flow.context: In this step of the Thirty-Roll Search you design your own plan for spending 30 rolls, and test it.

flow.do: 1. Put the two scores side by side. 2. Ask which plan came closer to the truth, and why. 3. Ask what a real fossil hunter could do that is like searching layer 20 again.
flow.say: Which plan gave the smaller total gap? Why? What could a real scientist do that is like rolling again for the top layer?
flow.kid: Compare the two scores. Which plan was closer to the truth? Say why.

check.q: You want to know when a rare species really ended. Where should most of your searching go?
options: The top layers, searched again and again
check.why: The question is about the end, so the top layers matter most, and a rare species needs many searches for one find. If you chose every layer equally, you spent rolls on layers that cannot change the answer.

flow.parent: One good plan can lose to luck in a single try. If there is time, run each plan twice. A real scientist searches the same layer in many cliffs and digs more rock from the layers just below the boundary.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Thirty-Roll Search. You compare your own search plan with the equal plan and explain the difference.

items.p: What is a mass extinction?
opts: Most species on Earth ending within a short time
One species ending in one forest
Many animals dying in one cold winter
A species moving to a new place
items.why: A mass extinction ends most species, all over the world, in a short stretch of geological time. One hard winter kills many animals but ends no species.

items.p: The slow, steady ending of species in normal times is called ____ extinction.
items.why: A few species end in every million years, even when nothing unusual happens. That steady loss is the background.

items.p: True or false: most of the species that ever lived are still alive today.
items.why: False. Scientists estimate that more than 99 out of 100 species that ever lived are extinct. They did not all live at the same time.

items.p: Put the five mass extinctions in order, oldest first.
items.why: They happened about 444, 370, 252, 201 and 66 million years ago.

items.p: Match each mass extinction to a likely cause.
items.why: Each one had a different cause. In each, the air, the sea or the climate changed too fast for most species.
pairs: ice sheets and a falling sea
an asteroid strike, with eruptions in India

items.p: Which rare metal in a thin clay layer was the first clue to an asteroid strike?
items.why: Asteroids hold far more iridium than Earth's surface rocks. Iron is common in ordinary rock, so it would be no clue.

items.p: Sort these by what happened to them 66 million years ago.
items.why: Large animals and those who depended on fresh plants or floating algae ended. Small animals with shelter, and those in rivers, mostly lived.

items.p: On a full board of 36 squares, no group could add a new species. Explain why.
items.a: A new species needs an empty niche to live in. On the full board every square was taken, so there was no room, whatever the die showed.
items.why: A strong answer says that the limit was room, not the die or the group.

items.p: True or false: after a mass extinction, the lost species come back.
items.why: False. A lost species never returns. New and different species arise from the survivors.

items.p: Which land animals mostly survived the asteroid strike?
opts: Small ones with shelter who ate insects or seeds
items.why: Small animals need little food, and insects and seeds were still there. Choosing the largest animals mixes up strength with what the dark months demanded.

items.p: A species thought to be extinct and then found alive is called a ____ species.
items.why: The coelacanth and Jerdon's courser are Lazarus species. Each was missed for a very long time.

items.p: Draw a cliff of rock layers with one boundary layer. Show different fossils below and above the boundary.
items.a: A cliff with several layers and one thin dark layer. The fossils below, such as ammonites, differ from the fossils above.
items.why: A boundary layer marks a change of age. A strong drawing shows that some fossils stop at the layer and do not appear above.
items.art: A blank outline of a cliff with horizontal layers.

items.p: Five species end on the same day. Why is the last fossil of the rarest one found lower in the cliff?
items.a: A rare species leaves few fossils. In many layers they were alive and no fossil was found. So their last fossil lies below the layer where they really ended.
items.why: A strong answer separates two things: when the species lived, and where a fossil happened to be found.

items.p: Three of these ended 66 million years ago. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: The nautilus lived on in deep water and is alive today. The other three ended.

items.p: Two children argue about extinct animals.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives evidence, such as how long the big dinosaurs or the trilobites lasted. It also says what the other child has right: some species do end because rivals do better.
items.why: The second child is closer to what the rocks show for mass extinctions. In normal times, though, a species can lose out to others, so the first child is not wholly wrong.

views.says: Extinct animals failed. Something was wrong with them.
They fitted their world well. Their world changed too fast.

items.ask: Which child do you agree with? Give one piece of evidence. Then say one thing the other child has right.

worksheets.title: Who Survives, and How We Know (stretch)

items.p: Why did shell-building sea animals suffer most at the end of the Permian?
opts: Dissolved carbon dioxide made the sea more acid
items.why: Carbon dioxide from the eruptions dissolved in the sea and made a weak acid. Shells are harder to build in more acid water. There were no people or boats then.

items.p: Great size helped dinosaurs for millions of years. Explain why it became a danger after the asteroid strike.
items.a: A large body needs a lot of food every day. With sunlight blocked, plants died and food ran out. Large animals starved first. Small animals needed little and could shelter.
items.why: A strong answer links size to food, and says that the same feature can help in one world and harm in another.

items.p: Match each word to its meaning.
items.why: These four words are needed to describe what happens before and after a mass extinction.
pairs: a way of making a living in a place
the growth of species numbers after an extinction
a thin rock layer between two ages

items.p: True or false: mammals first appeared after the big dinosaurs died out.
items.why: False. Mammals lived beside the dinosaurs for well over 100 million years. They were mostly small until the big dinosaurs ended.

items.p: Put these in order, starting from the asteroid strike.
a: Dust and soot block the Sun
items.why: Darkness came first. Ferns grew from spores, then forests returned. Large mammals appeared hundreds of thousands of years later.
items: Dust and soot block the Sun

items.p: In a refill game, a group holding 2 squares may add at most 2 more. What does this rule stand for?
opts: New species arise only from living species
items.why: Each new species splits off from one that already exists. So a group with few species can add only a few at a time.

items.p: The splitting of one group into many new species that fill empty niches is an adaptive ____.
items.why: After the big dinosaurs ended, mammals went through an adaptive radiation into bats, whales, horses and many more.

items.p: Sort each piece of evidence by the cause it points to.
items.why: A shock, a crater and melted beads come from a strike. Lava and heat-trapping gases come from eruptions.
items: a clay layer rich in iridium
lava covering much of western India
gases that warm the whole Earth

items.p: The last fossil of a rare animal lies five metres below a boundary layer. Give two possible explanations.
items.a: One: the animal ended earlier than the others. Two: the animal lived right up to the boundary, and no fossil from the top five metres has been found yet.
items.why: Both are possible. More searching in more places is the way to tell them apart.

items.p: Draw a time line from 500 million years ago to now. Label the five mass extinctions on it.
a: End of the Ordovician, about 444 million years ago
Late Devonian, about 370 million years ago
End of the Permian, about 252 million years ago
End of the Triassic, about 201 million years ago
End of the Cretaceous, about 66 million years ago
items.why: The gaps between them are uneven. Mass extinctions do not come on a timetable.
items.art: A blank horizontal line with '500 million years ago' at the left end and 'now' at the right end.

items.p: About how long did the number of species take to recover after past extinctions?
items.why: A study of the whole record of sea life found about 10 million years. That is more than 30 times as long as our species has existed.

items.p: True or false: a species that nobody has seen for 50 years must be extinct.
items.why: False. Jerdon's courser was missed for 86 years and found alive. Small, rare animals who are active at night are easy to miss.

items.p: Two scientists argue about what ended the big dinosaurs.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and names evidence. For the asteroid: the crater, the iridium layer and shocked quartz, all of the right age. For the volcanoes: the huge Deccan lava flows and their gases. It may also say that both played a part.
items.why: Most scientists think the asteroid was the main cause. The lava is hard to date exactly, so the share of each is still argued.

views.says: The asteroid did it. The crater and the iridium layer are the right age.
The Deccan eruptions did it. Their gases changed the air for thousands of years.

items.ask: Which scientist do you agree with more? Give two pieces of evidence. What would change your mind?

items.p: Three of these have been linked to mass extinctions. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Ice, lava floods and an asteroid changed the whole Earth's air, sea or climate. A predator hunting prey is part of normal life and ends no species by itself.

items.p: Why were rivers and lakes hit less hard than the open sea after the strike?
opts: Dead matter washed in from the land fed them
The dust did not reach rivers
items.why: River food chains can run on dead leaves and other detritus from the land. Food chains of the open sea begin with floating algae, who need light.

items.p: Normally 2 species in 10,000 end every 100 years. How many of 40,000 species should end in 100 years?
items.why: This is the expected number for normal times. Real losses are compared with it.

items.p: Since 1900, 477 species were lost where 9 were expected. About how many times the normal number is that?
items.why: 477 ÷ 9 = 53, which is about 50 times. Subtracting 9 from 477 gives the extra losses, not how many times.

items.p: Two scientists argue about what to call today's extinctions.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and uses numbers. For 'already begun': losses are about 50 times normal, and over one in four checked species are at risk. For 'not yet': fewer than 1 in 100 named species are recorded lost, and a mass extinction means 3 in 4.
items.why: The two agree on the facts and on the danger. They differ on the word. Seeing that is part of a strong answer.

views.says: A sixth mass extinction has already begun. The rate is far above normal.
It has not happened yet. Most species are still here, so it can be prevented.

items.ask: Which scientist do you agree with? Use at least one number. What do the two agree on?

items.p: Someone says: 'Extinction is natural, so losing species today does not matter.' Answer with two facts.
items.a: Recovery after past extinctions took about 10 million years, far longer than people have existed. A lost species never comes back. Also, today's losses are many times the natural rate, and their cause is people, who can choose to stop.
items.why: A strong answer accepts what is true in the claim, that extinction is natural, and then shows what the claim leaves out.

items.p: True or false: the five great mass extinctions are the only times many species died out together.
items.why: False. The record shows many smaller extinction events too. The five are the largest of them.

items.p: What is the Signor-Lipps effect?
opts: Rare fossils stop below a species' real end
Fossils sink through rock over time
items.why: The last fossil found is older than the last animal, and more so for rare species. So a sudden ending can look slow. Fossils do not move down through solid rock.

items.p: Match each finding to what it most likely means.
items.why: Each finding is evidence. A scientist asks what would have to be true for the rocks to look this way.
pairs: No trilobites above one layer, anywhere
Fern spores crowd the rock above a layer
bare ground was being covered again
Mammal fossils get bigger above a layer

items.p: Three species end together. Order them by how close their last fossil is likely to be to the true end.
a: Found on a roll of 1 to 5
Found on a roll of 1 to 3
Found only on a roll of 1
items.why: The more often a species is found, the smaller the gap between the last fossil and the true end.
items: Found only on a roll of 1
Found on a roll of 1 to 5
Found on a roll of 1 to 3

items.p: Draw a branching tree of life. Show a mass extinction cutting most branches, and what grows afterwards.
items.a: A tree with many branches. A line across the tree ends most of them. A few branches pass the line and split into many new twigs. The cut branches do not regrow.
items.why: A strong drawing shows three things: most branches end, a few continue, and the new twigs come only from those few.
items.art: A blank page with a small trunk drawn at the bottom.

items.p: Suppose the asteroid had missed the Earth. Why might humans never have appeared?
opts: Big dinosaurs would have kept the niches of large animals
The Earth would be too hot
items.why: Mammals already existed, but stayed small while big dinosaurs held the niches for large land animals. Large mammals, including apes, arose only after those niches emptied.

items.p: Unrelated animals arriving at the same answer to the same problem is called ____.
items.why: Dolphins and ichthyosaurs are unrelated, and both have the body shape of a fast fish. That is convergence.

items.p: Wings arose separately in insects, birds and bats. What does that suggest about replaying the history of life?
items.a: It suggests that some answers, like wings, are likely to appear again, because flying is a good way to live. It does not show that the same animals would appear. Birds and bats are very different flyers.
items.why: A strong answer uses the evidence for convergence and also sees its limit. Similar answers can come from very different beings.

items.p: Sort these statements: agreed by scientists, or still argued?
items.why: The events themselves are agreed. The shares of blame, the right name for today, and the cause of the Devonian extinction are still argued.
items: An asteroid struck 66 million years ago
Which did more killing, asteroid or eruptions
Species are ending faster than normal today
Whether today is a mass extinction yet
Why the Late Devonian extinction came in steps

items.p: True or false: the first fossil found of a species shows exactly when that species began.
items.why: False. The first animals of a species lived before the first one that was buried, kept and found. The gap works at the start just as at the end.

items.p: Three of these help a living species stay unseen for decades. Which is the odd one out?
opts: Being large and living near towns
items.why: A large animal near towns is seen often. Night habits, deep water and small numbers all make a species easy to miss.

opts: A few species end in every million years
Most species end in a short time
quiz.why: Background extinction is the slow, steady loss of normal times. Most species ending in a short time is a mass extinction.

quiz.p: Which of these would count as a mass extinction?
opts: Three quarters of all species end within a short time
A lake dries and one fish species ends
A flood kills many animals in one state
A forest loses half of the trees
quiz.why: A mass extinction ends most species across the world. A flood or a lost forest kills many living beings, but that is different from ending most species.

quiz.p: Which mass extinction was the largest?
quiz.why: About 8 in 10 sea species ended about 252 million years ago. The end of the Cretaceous is the best known, because of the dinosaurs, but was smaller.

quiz.p: Which mass extinction has clear signs of an asteroid strike?
quiz.why: The crater and the iridium layer are both 66 million years old. The end of the Permian is linked to eruptions in Siberia.

quiz.p: After a mass extinction, where do the new species come from?
quiz.why: Every new species splits off from a living one. That is why the group you wiped out never returned to your board.

quiz.p: Why do new species arise faster after a mass extinction than before?
quiz.why: With few rivals, more varieties can live and have young, and natural selection fits them to the empty niches. Trying harder does not change what is inherited.

quiz.p: Which animal was most likely to survive the asteroid strike?
quiz.why: A small animal needs little food, insects lived on, and a burrow gave shelter. Giants starved, and the forests that treetop birds needed were lost.

quiz.p: In the dark months, why did food chains that begin with dead leaves keep going?
opts: Dead matter was there without sunlight
Dead leaves make their own food
quiz.why: Fallen leaves and wood were already lying there, so the animals who eat them still had food. Chains that begin with living plants stopped when the plants could not make food.

quiz.p: A rare species' last fossil lies eight layers below a boundary. What is the fairest conclusion?
opts: They may have lived up to the boundary
They surely ended eight layers early
quiz.why: Rare species leave gaps, so the last fossil is usually below the real end. Choosing 'surely ended early' reads the gap as the truth.

quiz.p: Which finding points to an asteroid and not to volcanoes?
quiz.why: Only a huge sudden shock cracks quartz in that way. Lava points to volcanoes, and fern spores and warming fit both causes.

quiz.p: What do scientists agree about extinction today?
opts: Species are ending faster than normal, because of people
Three quarters of species are already gone
The rate is the same as always
quiz.why: The rate is many times the normal one, and the causes are things people do. But most species are still alive, so three quarters gone is wrong.

quiz.p: Fewer than 1 in 100 named species are recorded as lost. Why are scientists still worried?
opts: The rate of loss is far above normal
quiz.why: If such a high rate went on for a few thousand years, the losses would reach the level of the five great extinctions. No large asteroid is known to be on its way.

applications: People who protect wildlife must decide when to stop searching for a missing species. They use the idea from the Last Fossil Test: a rare species can go unseen for a long time and still be alive.
Geologists who search for oil and gas use tiny fossils and boundary layers to tell the age of rock deep under the ground. The Chicxulub crater was first noticed by two men searching for oil.
Space agencies track large rocks that pass near the Earth. In 2022 the DART spacecraft struck a small asteroid and changed its path, as a first test of pushing one aside.
Scientists who study the sea measure how acid the water is, year after year. They compare today's change with the change at the end of the Permian.
Seed banks keep dry seeds for many years. A dry seed can wait through a bad time, as seeds did after the asteroid strike.
Climate scientists test their computer models on the great warmings of the past. If a model can reproduce what the rocks record, people can trust its forecasts more.
The Red List tells governments which species need help first. India used such counts to plan the protection of tigers, lions and rhinoceroses.

open_questions.q: How much of the killing 66 million years ago was done by the asteroid, and how much by the Deccan eruptions?
open_questions.why_open: The two happened within a few hundred thousand years of each other. The lava is hard to date exactly, and two methods give different orders for the biggest flows.

open_questions.q: Why did the Late Devonian extinction come in several steps?
open_questions.why_open: There are several ideas, such as the spread of the first forests, eruptions and changes in the sea. The rocks of that age are old and worn, so the evidence is thin.

open_questions.q: How many species are alive on Earth today?
open_questions.why_open: About two million have been named. Estimates of the real number run from a few million to many millions. Without that number, the count of species being lost is also uncertain.

open_questions.q: If the history of life ran again, would beings like us appear?
open_questions.why_open: Nobody can run the test. Some scientists point to chance events such as the asteroid, and others point to the many times the same body forms have arisen.

open_questions.q: Why do some groups survive a mass extinction and then fade away over the next few million years?
open_questions.why_open: It may be that too few species of the group were left, or that the new world no longer suited them. The fossil record is often too thin to tell.

open_questions.q: Which species listed as extinct are still alive somewhere?
open_questions.why_open: Nobody can search everywhere. Small, rare animals of the night, the deep sea and thick forest are missed for decades.
