maths.problem: On your paper time line, 1 centimetre stands for 10 million years. The end-Ordovician extinction was 444 million years ago. How far from 'now' do you draw the line? Which is the bigger gap on the strip: Ordovician to Devonian, or Triassic to Cretaceous?
maths.answer: 44.4 centimetres from 'now'. The gap from the Triassic to the Cretaceous is bigger.
maths.explain: 444 ÷ 10 = 44.4 centimetres. Ordovician to Devonian is 444 − 370 = 74 million years, which is 7.4 centimetres. Triassic to Cretaceous is 201 − 66 = 135 million years, which is 13.5 centimetres. So the second gap is nearly twice as long.
maths.context: This is about Five Marks on a Paper Road. There you make a paper strip where 1 centimetre stands for 10 million years, and mark the five mass extinctions on it.
maths.why_maths: A scale turns times too long to imagine into lengths you can see and compare. The uneven gaps show that mass extinctions do not come on a timetable.

maths.problem: Before the extinction, mammals held 4 of the 36 squares on the board. When the board was full again, they held 12. What fraction of the board did they hold each time? The mammals had the same die before and after. So what made the difference?
maths.answer: One ninth before, and one third after. The difference was empty squares next to them.
maths.explain: 4 out of 36 is 4 ÷ 36 = one ninth. 12 out of 36 is 12 ÷ 36 = one third. One third is three times one ninth. The die and the mammals did not change. The extinction emptied the squares around them, and that gave them room.
maths.context: This is about the Empty Board Test. There a grid of 36 squares stands for the world, and you refill it with a die after a mass extinction. These are made-up results.

chart.title: Made-up example results: squares held by each group

maths.why_maths: A fraction shows a group's share of the whole world. Comparing the shares before and after shows how much an extinction can change who fills the world.

maths.problem: In the Last Fossil Test, the rarest species is found only on a roll of 1. What is the chance of a find in any one layer? About how many layers must you search, on average, for one find? A species found on a roll of 1, 2 or 3 would need about how many?
maths.answer: The chance is 1 in 6. You need about 6 layers on average for the rarest species, and about 2 layers for the other.
maths.explain: A die has 6 faces and only one of them is a 1, so the chance is 1 in 6. On average one find comes in every 6 tries. Rolls of 1, 2 or 3 are 3 faces out of 6, which is 1 in 2, so about 2 tries. That is why the last fossil of the rarest species usually lies about 5 layers below the top, and the other lies about 1 layer below.
maths.context: This is about the Last Fossil Test. There you search a paper cliff of 20 layers with a die, to find the last fossil of five species who all ended at the top.
maths.why_maths: Chance tells you how big a gap to expect between the last fossil and the true end. Scientists use the same reasoning to estimate when a species really ended.

maths.problem: At the normal rate, about 9 species of animals with backbones should have ended since 1900. On a cautious count, 477 have. How many times the normal number is that? What fraction of the 40,000 species checked is 477, roughly?
maths.answer: 53 times. About 1 in 84, which is a little more than 1 in 100.
maths.explain: 477 ÷ 9 = 53. For the fraction, 40,000 ÷ 477 is about 84, so 477 is about 1 part in 84. The two answers go together. Species are ending about 50 times faster than normal, and yet about 83 out of every 84 are still here.
maths.context: This is about Fifty Times Faster. There you colour 9 squares for the normal number of species lost since 1900, and 477 squares for the real number.
maths.why_maths: Dividing shows two different things: how fast the losses are, and how large they are so far. Mixing up the two is the most common mistake in talk about extinction.

maths.problem: After past extinctions, the number of species took about 10 million years to recover. Our species is about 300,000 years old. How many times longer is the recovery than the whole time people have existed?
maths.explain: 10,000,000 ÷ 300,000 is the same as 100 ÷ 3, which is about 33. So people would have to exist 33 times longer than they have so far, to see one full recovery.
maths.context: This is about the Empty Board Test. There the board refills in a few rounds. In the real world, each round stands for a very long time.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two big numbers answers a question about life: could people wait for nature to recover from a mass extinction? The division says no.

maths.problem: The number of filled squares after each round was 9, 17, 27, 33 and 36. Work out how many squares were added in each round. In which round was the refill fastest? Why did it slow down at the end?
maths.answer: 8, 10, 6 and 3 squares were added. Round 2 was fastest. It slowed because few empty squares were left.
maths.explain: 17 − 9 = 8, 27 − 17 = 10, 33 − 27 = 6, and 36 − 33 = 3. At first there are few species to split, so growth is moderate. Then more species means more new ones each round. At the end almost no empty squares are left, and some cannot be reached. A line chart of these numbers bends into the shape of a stretched letter S.
maths.context: This is about the Empty Board Test. There you count the filled squares on a 36-square board after each round of refilling. These are made-up results.

chart.title: Made-up example results: filled squares after each round

maths.why_maths: The differences between the numbers show how the speed of recovery changes. The pattern, slow, then fast, then slow, also appears in the real fossil record.

warmup.q: How many great mass extinctions do scientists count?
Which was the largest, and what caused it?
warmup.a: The end of the Permian, about 252 million years ago. Huge eruptions in Siberia warmed the Earth and made the sea acid.

warmup.q: Name two clues that an asteroid struck 66 million years ago.
warmup.a: A clay layer rich in iridium, and a buried crater in Mexico. Quartz with shock cracks is a third.

warmup.q: Do lost species come back after a mass extinction?
warmup.a: No. New species arise from the survivors.

warmup.q: Why is the last fossil of a species not the last animal?
warmup.a: Few animals become fossils and few fossils are found, so the species lived on after the last one we have.

warmup.q: What is a Lazarus species? Name one.
warmup.a: A species thought extinct and found alive, such as the coelacanth or Jerdon's courser.

warmup.q: About how long does the number of species take to recover after an extinction?

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that an asteroid struck at the end of the age of dinosaurs? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: For 150 years, most geologists held that the Earth changes only slowly. Charles Lyell taught this in the 1830s, and Charles Darwin agreed. They thought sudden mass deaths in the rocks were only gaps in the record. In the late 1970s Walter Alvarez was studying a thin clay layer at Gubbio in Italy. Below it lay tiny sea fossils of the dinosaurs' time, and above it almost none. He asked his father, the physicist Luis Alvarez, how to tell how long the clay took to form. They decided to measure iridium, which falls from space as dust at a steady rate. The chemists Helen Michel and Frank Asaro did the measuring. The clay held about thirty times more iridium than the rock around it. That was far too much for slow dust. In 1980 the four proposed that an asteroid had struck. Many geologists objected and asked where the crater was. In fact Glen Penfield and Antonio Camargo, who were searching for oil in Mexico, had found a buried ring 180 kilometres wide in 1978. Almost nobody listened to them. In 1991 Alan Hildebrand's team connected the ring to the clay.
how_we_found_out.who: Walter Alvarez, Luis Alvarez, Helen Michel and Frank Asaro in California. Glen Penfield and Antonio Camargo, and later Alan Hildebrand, for the crater.
how_we_found_out.when: The iridium paper came out in 1980. The crater was first noticed in 1978 and confirmed in 1991.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the Earth and its life change only slowly, so a sudden worldwide die-off could not be real. The iridium layer and the crater showed that one day can change the history of life.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman chemist in a 1970s laboratory holding a small sample tube up to the light, with a striped piece of rock showing a thin dark clay line on the bench beside her.

roots.context: We have learned how most kinds of life ended five times, and how the survivors filled the world again. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Empty Board Test, no group could add a species while the board was full. The extinction emptied most squares, and the few survivors filled them within a few rounds. The group that had held most of the board never came back. So the species alive today are not the best that ever lived. They descend from whoever got through, and they grew into the room that the lost ones left.
deep_truth.habit: We speak of extinct animals as failures. We say 'dead as a dodo', and we call something old-fashioned a dinosaur. We speak as if living species had won a fair race. But the big dinosaurs filled the land for more than 130 million years, and ended because the world changed in a day. Calling the living 'winners' and the extinct 'losers' hides how much depended on what the world did.
deep_truth.evidence: On your board, the mammals held 4 squares for as long as the board was full. They held about 12 after the refill, and in some runs they held none. In the real record, no land animal with a backbone heavier than about 25 kilograms came through the asteroid strike, except some crocodiles and turtles. Mammals stayed small beside the dinosaurs for more than 100 million years. Within about 700,000 years of the strike, some weighed nearly 50 kilograms.

three.who_am_i: You are a mammal. Your ancestors of 66 million years ago were small animals who got through the dark months, perhaps in burrows. If the asteroid had missed the Earth, there might be no people at all.
three.what_is_life: Almost every species ends, yet life has not stopped once in more than 3,500 million years. Life goes on by branching into new species from whoever is left.
three.what_is_this_world: The world changes. The sea, the air and the climate shift, sometimes slowly and sometimes in a day. Living beings change them too. The first forests did, and people are doing so now.

roots.thread: All living beings descend from one beginning. Over a very long time, that one line branched into millions of species. Five times, most of the branches were cut off together. Each time the line of life itself was not cut. The few branches left grew and split, and the world was full of many kinds again. They were different kinds each time. So the many kinds are not fixed. They come and go, and the one line of life runs on through all of them. You are part of that line.

teachings.teaching: Thiruvalluvar says that someone who was here yesterday is gone today, and that this is the way of the world.
teachings.link: Thiruvalluvar is speaking of one person. The rocks show the same thing for whole species. Species that filled the seas for millions of years are missing from the next layer up.

teachings.source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura (On the Nature of Things), Book 5, lines 855 to 877
teachings.teaching: The Roman poet Lucretius wrote, about 2,000 years ago, that many kinds of living beings must have died out long ago because they could not go on leaving young.
teachings.link: Lucretius reasoned his way to extinction without a single fossil. It took until about 1800 for scientists to show, with mammoth teeth, that he was right.

teachings.teaching: Lao Tzu says that all things rise and flourish, and each one then returns to the root it came from.
teachings.link: After each mass extinction, new species grew from the few lines that were left. In the Empty Board Test you saw the board fill again from a handful of squares.

science.text: Every living being today descends from ancestors who lived through all five mass extinctions.
If the history of life ran again, the living world would be very different. Others say it would be much the same in its main shapes.

other_view.who: David Raup, an American palaeontologist, in Extinction: Bad Genes or Bad Luck? (1991)
other_view.view: Raup studied extinction for most of his life. He concluded that species mostly end through bad luck. A species can be well fitted to the world and still be struck by a kind of trouble that their ancestors had not met before. In his view there is no thread and no balance in it. An extinction is simply a loss, and what comes after is whatever happens to come.

practice.title: Three who came through
practice.say: Let's sit by a window. Find one bird, one plant and your own hand. Look at the bird first. That bird is a living dinosaur, and her ancestors came through the asteroid strike. Breathe in and out once, slowly. Now look at the plant. Their ancestors waited through the dark as seeds or spores. Breathe in and out once. Now look at your hand. Your ancestors were small mammals, hiding and eating insects. Breathe in and out once. All three of you come from survivors. All three of you share one family, far back.
practice.kid: Sit by a window. Find a bird, a plant and your own hand. Look at each one in turn. Take one slow breath for each. Say quietly: your ancestors came through. Then say: so did mine.

ask: On your board, did the mammals earn the empty squares, or were they given them?
The trilobites lasted 270 million years and then ended. Were they a success or a failure?
If the asteroid had missed, who do you think would be looking out of your window today?
The dodo is gone and the Nicobar pigeon is here. Is anything of the dodo still alive?

playtest: The experiments, activities and games were reasoned through step by step for a city flat, and the two dice experiments were also run 2,000 times on a computer to see what results to expect. They have not yet been tried at home. The Empty Board Test (core) needs only paper, a pencil, an eraser, a coin and a die. In the computer runs the board filled in 3 to 6 rounds almost every time. The mammals ended with 12 squares on average, anywhere from 0 to more than 20. In about 1 run in 16, every mammal square is rubbed out by the coin. That is a real result and worth talking about. The Last Fossil Test needs a die and paper. In the computer runs the rarest species' last fossil lay about 5 layers below the top on average. It was in the top layer about 1 time in 6, so one cliff alone can mislead, and the steps ask for three cliffs. In Three Rules for Survival the scores should come out as 9, 11 and 12 out of 13. The Dark Week needs whole green moong and takes eight days. The dark seedlings should be tall, thin and pale by day 6, and too much water brings mould, so the step says what to do. The numbers in the made-up results agree across the experiments, the maths and the worksheets. Facts were checked by web search on 19 Nov 2026. A grown-up may want to check these again: the size of the gap below the iridium layer where dinosaur bones were first missing, Peter Ward's ammonite searches in Spain, the idea of a companion star and why it was dropped, the last sure sighting of the slender-billed curlew, and the counts of living mammal and bird species. The three films were confirmed by title and channel, and nobody has watched them from here. A parent should watch them first. The Fossil Museum at Varanavasi may keep short hours, so ring before you go.
